Instrumental tango by Osvaldo Pugliese, 1946. MusicBrainz and a 78 rpm archive page date the first recording to 21 August 1946 in Buenos Aires, Odeon, matrix 15758. English Wikipedia calls it Pugliese's signature rhythmic tango. The title is an onomatopoeia for the bandoneon attack. Bibletango gives the composition date as 1943, which is not followed here because the recording sources and Wikipedia use 1946.

Zamba by the Mendoza businessman Luis Hermenegildo Profili, registered at SADAIC on 24 April 1964 under the pseudonym Luis H. Morales and the title De mi esperanza. Jorge Cafrune's recording on Emoción, canto y guitarra (CBS, 1964) spread it. Los Chalchaleros recorded it in 1965 as De mi esperanza. Listeners renamed it from the first line. Profili was from San Martín, Mendoza, not from the Northwest.

León Gieco wrote it in 1978 in Cañada Rosquín, Santa Fe. The Spanish song page and the album page 4.º L.P. say the album was released in 1979; English Wikipedia calls 4to. LP a 1978 album. The album page describes a studio take with bandoneonist Dino Saluzzi during the 1978 sessions. Year 1978 is the composition year. Radio Nacional has a page dated 26 July 1979 about registration of the song; that page was seen in search but is a short notice.

Edmundo P. Zaldívar, a Buenos Aires guitarist, composed this carnavalito in 1941 on the way to Radio El Mundo, before he had visited the Northwest. La Nación reports a 1943 piano-sheet cover that calls it a carnavalito and danza típica indo criolla. The Universidad Nacional del Litoral catalogue lists a piano score, Buenos Aires, Tierra Linda, about 1943. A Jujuy decree of 30 September 1954 declared it regional music and dance of the province. Year is the composition year given in the biography and in La Nación.

Los Chalchaleros, formed in Salta, debuted on 16 June 1948 at Teatro Alberdi. The group article says the first song they sang in public was Zamba del grillo by Atahualpa Yupanqui. The composition year of Yupanqui's zamba is not given on the pages consulted. Year is the debut performance year. A second page was used only to confirm the group's later folklore role, not this title.

Included on Las últimas composiciones (RCA Victor, November 1966). Spanish Wikipedia says the song was composed in 1962 and released on that 1966 album. Year is the release year. English Wikipedia also treats it as Parra's song from that album.

Violeta Parra's Spanish Wikipedia biography says the 1959 Odeon albums La tonada and La cueca include her setting of her brother Nicanor Parra's poem Cueca larga de los Meneses. A second page consulted confirms her as a nueva canción composer but does not discuss this title. Year is the album year given in the biography.

Spanish Wikipedia says Víctor Jara composed the song in 1969. It is on the album Pongo en tus manos abiertas... and is the B-side of the 1969 Jota Jota single whose A-side is Plegaria a un labrador. On that single the B-side is sung by Jara alone. The names Amanda and Manuel in the lyric are his parents' names, according to the song article.

title_original: El derecho de vivir en paz
title_english: The Right to Live in Peace
research_notes: Title song of Víctor Jara's sixth solo album, DICAP, April 1971. The Fundación Víctor Jara lists it as track 1 of the original edition. The song article says it was written in 1969 as a protest against the Vietnam War. The album page says most songs are by Jara and names Plegaria a un labrador, not this title, as the piece composed with Patricio Castillo. Electric guitars and organ come from the collaboration with Los Blops. Year is the album release year.

A-side of the 1969 Jota Jota single JJS-101, sung by Víctor Jara with Quilapayún. The single page credits Víctor Jara and Patricio Castillo. The 1971 album article says Plegaria a un labrador was composed together with Patricio Castillo, and the Fundación track list includes it on side B of the 1971 LP. Year is the single year.

title_original: El pueblo unido jamás será vencido
title_english: The People United Will Never Be Defeated
research_notes: Music by Sergio Ortega; the text is credited to Sergio Ortega and Quilapayún. Quilapayún's official song page and press page document a 1973 premiere, but they do not agree on the day: one account says 21 June 1973 and another places a debut on the Alameda in August 1973. An academic paper by Karmy and Farías places the composition in mid-1973 in Santiago. The studio recording is dated 1974 on the official site. Year is 1973 for the composition and public premiere, not the studio date.

title_original: El baile de los que sobran
title_english: The Dance of Those Left Over
original_instruments: Voice | Electric guitar | Drum machine | Synthesizer
research_notes: Written by Jorge González for Los Prisioneros' album Pateando piedras (EMI Odeón Chilena, 1986). Memoria Chilena, the National Library of Chile, and both Wikipedia language editions date the song to 1986 and credit González. He has described writing it with a small drum machine and a Casio keyboard, with acoustic guitar by Claudio Narea added later.

Paseo vallenato by Emiliano Zuleta Baquero, 1938, from a piqueria with Lorenzo Morales (Moralito). Spanish and English Wikipedia and a La Tercera article agree on Zuleta and 1938. Guillermo Buitrago later recorded a version as Que Criterio and claimed authorship. Carlos Vives's 1990s recording made it an international hit; that version is a later cover, not the original record.

Juan Madera Castro wrote the instrumental cumbia in 1960 while playing clarinet in Pedro Salcedo's orchestra; Wilson Choperena added the lyric months later. Spanish Wikipedia says the definitive version is the Discos Tropical 78 rpm recorded in Barranquilla in 1961, with Choperena singing and Madera on clarinet. The work was notarised on 24 October 1962. English Wikipedia has given a later date for the lyric. Year is the 1961 Tropical recording. A 2010 court ruling treated Madera and Choperena as co-authors, with Madera as composer.

Salsa by Joe Arroyo, recorded with La Verdad on the album Musa Original (Discos Fuentes, 1986). English Wikipedia dates the song to 1986 and notes its relation to his earlier piece El Mulato (1978). The artist site lists the album and the track. The site's editorial dates are from 2026 and are not used as the song's year. Also known by the subtitle No le pegue a la negra.

Cumbia by José Benito Barros. Semana and Radio Enciclopedia say he finished it in the late 1960s and that the first recording was by Trío Los Inseparables in 1969. English Wikipedia identifies the song and the composer and does not give a year. Year is the first-recording year from the magazine and radio accounts.

Cumbia by Lucho Bermúdez, from his 1970 CBS album of the same name, with vocals by Matilde Díaz. English and Spanish Wikipedia agree on the composer, the year and the singer. Later use in the film Encanto is a reuse of a 1970 popular song, not the song's origin.

Vals by María Isabel Granda Larco (Chabuca Granda). Spanish Wikipedia and the Peruvian Ministry of Culture agree that she signed it on 7 January 1950 and that it was premiered on 21 July 1950. The first recording cited on the Spanish page is Los Morochucos in 1953. English Wikipedia gives a conflicting 1950 recording date for Los Morochucos. Year is the 1950 composition and premiere.

Vals by Felipe Pinglo Alva. Spanish Wikipedia places the composition in the early 1930s, a possible premiere in 1931 by Alcides Carreño and Pedro Espinel at Teatro Alfonso XIII in Callao, publication of the lyric in El Cancionero de Lima in 1934, and the first disc by Los Trovadores del Perú in 1943 (Odeón, Buenos Aires). The melody was later confused with the Argentine waltz Mi Marta. Year is left empty because the sources do not settle a single composition year.

Afro-Peruvian song from San Luis de Cañete. Spanish Wikipedia says Perú Negro staged Caitro Soto's version in the early 1970s and published it on the 1973 album Gran Premio del Festival Hispanoamericano de la Danza y la Canción. Celia Cruz recorded a salsa version in 1974. No composition year is stated. Year is the 1973 album. The melody is treated as traditional, with Soto as the arranger of the version Perú Negro used.

Huayno from Cusco. The melody was written in 1942 by Miguel Ángel Hurtado Delgado as Tusuy; his brother Evencio wrote the Quechua lyric, and the song was entered in a 1945 Cusco folklore contest under the name Valicha, for Valeriana Huillca. Instituto Raíces and RPP tell that sequence. Spanish Wikipedia's publication year and English Wikipedia's 1945 writing date do not match. Year 1945 is the contest year of the known Quechua song.

Joropo from the zarzuela Alma llanera. Music by Pedro Elías Gutiérrez, lyric by Rafael Bolívar Coronado. Premiered on 19 September 1914 at Teatro Caracas. The Banda Marcial de Caracas played it in public on 31 December 1914 at Plaza Bolívar. First printed in 1915. The Venezuelan culture ministry and the National Library document the centenary of that premiere. Sources say it draws on the joropo Marisela and the waltz Mita. Filed here as Venezuelan joropo repertoire; the zarzuela origin is noted.

Pasaje by Simón Díaz, not a joropo. Track B1 of the 1980 album Golpe y Pasaje (Palacio LPS-66479). Recorded at Audio Uno in Caracas with the Conjunto Criollo de Cándido Herrera. Spanish and English Wikipedia and the Sincopa LP note agree on Díaz, the title and 1980. Later use of verses by the Gipsy Kings is a separate adaptation.

English Wikipedia says the joropo was written in 1958 and first recorded that year by Mario Suárez for Kubaney, and that Hugo Blanco's 1961 recording was the hit. Spanish Wikipedia credits only José Manzo Perroni. MusicBrainz has listed both Manzo Perroni and Hugo Blanco. The composer field is left empty because the sources do not agree. Year 1958 is the first recording year given by English Wikipedia.

The Zitarrosa discography annex lists a 1968 Orfeo single (90003) with Doña Soledad on side A and the 1968 album Yo sé quién soy (Orfeo ULP 90504) with the song as track 2. A Radio Educación interview says he composed this candombe in 1969 while speaking from exile, which conflicts with the 1968 release. Year is the release year on the discography. Genre is taken from the interview, which calls it a candombe.

Opens the 1965 Tonal EP El canto de Zitarrosa (CP 5017). The discography annex lists it again on later Orfeo issues. The artist biography page identifies Zitarrosa but does not discuss this title, so the track credit rests on the discography. Genre follows the word milonga in the title and the EP's place in his early folk-song catalogue. A separate composer credit is not printed on the table.

Track on side B of the 1966 Tonal album Canta Zitarrosa (CP 040), repeated on the 1969 Orfeo issue of that album. The discography does not name a composer. Genre is taken from the title. Year is the first album year on the annex.

Guarania by José Asunción Flores. The lyric long associated with it is by Manuel Ortiz Guerrero; an earlier lyric by Rigoberto Fontao Meza was replaced. Flores and Ortiz Guerrero met in 1928. A decree of 24 July 1944 declared India an official song. No single composition year is stated on the pages consulted. The musicaparaguaya biography dates the creation of the guarania form to 1925 and, in another passage, questions the claim that Jejuí was the first work.

Named among Flores's early guaranias. English Wikipedia's guarania article calls Jejuí the first guarania. The musicaparaguaya.org.py biography says Flores created the guarania in 1925 and also prints a score caption that rejects the claim that Jejuí was his first work. Year is empty because of that conflict. The title is Guaraní.

Listed with the guaranias Flores wrote with Manuel Ortiz Guerrero after they met in 1928. The Spanish article glosses the title as Mariposa brillante. English Wikipedia's guarania overview names Panambí Vera among the best-known guaranias and does not give a year. Year is empty.

Music by Demetrio Ortiz, written in 1948 in Córdoba according to the Spanish article and Asunción City. Lyrics by Zulema de Mirkin, associated with a 1950 meeting in ABC Color's account. First performance cited as 1951. Year is the music year. The lyric is in Spanish and uses the Guaraní word kuñataĩ.

Asunción City says Demetrio Ortiz composed this guarania in 1943 in Concepción and dedicated it to his mother. The Folkways Harps of Paraguay booklet credits María Teresa Márquez and Demetrio Ortiz and does not give a year. English Wikipedia's guarania article names the song and does not date it. Year 1943 rests on Asunción City.

Paraguayan polca on Smithsonian Folkways SFW CD 40548, Harps of Paraguay (2009). The booklet says Pérez Cardozo used it to open his shows in Argentina. No composition year is printed. The 2009 date is the Folkways album, not the piece.

Paraguayan polca on Folkways SFW CD 40548. The booklet says Santiago Cortesi dedicated it to his hometown, Isla Saká in Caazapá. No composition year is given. Recorded there by Marcelo Rojas, harp, with guitar and bass.
Credited to Lorenzo Leguizamón on the Folkways SFW CD 40548 track list and described in the notes as a Paraguayan polca. No composition year is given.
Credited to Julián Alarcón on the Folkways SFW CD 40548 track list. The booklet classifies the album's harp pieces as Paraguayan polcas. No composition year is given.

Paraguayan polca by Félix Pérez Cardozo on Folkways SFW CD 40548. The notes say the harp imitates a bell, a train whistle and locomotive wheels, and that the piece refers to the train that brought milk into Asunción. No composition year is given.

Paraguayan polca by Herminio Giménez on Folkways SFW CD 40548. The booklet says he first conceived it for an orquesta típica and that the title joins Guaraní jeroky (dance) and popó (vivacious). No composition year is given.

Folkways SFW CD 40548 calls Pájaro campana anonymous and credits Félix Pérez Cardozo's harp arrangement. ABC Color and Portal Guaraní, citing a 1959 notarial statement, say Ampelio Villalba composed Guyra campana around 1914 and that Pérez Cardozo registered an arrangement of a popular motif. English Wikipedia has called it Pérez Cardozo's own composition; that claim is not followed here. Year is empty.
Credited to Prudencio Giménez on the Folkways SFW CD 40548 track list. No composition year is given. The album notes treat these harp pieces as Paraguayan polcas.
Paraguayan polca on Folkways SFW CD 40548. The booklet says harpist Alejandro Villamayor composed it for the town of Unión in San Pedro Department. No composition year is given.

Paraguayan polca by Digno García on Folkways SFW CD 40548. The notes describe a programmatic harp piece in 6/8 and name it with Pájaro campana and Tren lechero as a frequently played harp solo. No composition year is given.

Paraguayan polca on Folkways SFW CD 40548, credited to Kike Pedersen. The notes say maiteí means greetings in Guaraní and describe Pedersen combining traditional polca with a newer harmonic vocabulary. No composition year is given. The 2009 date is the album.

Folkways SFW CD 40548 calls this polca anonymous and associates it with popular festivities in the town of Paraguarí. No date is given. The booklet says it is often played for dance by a banda folclórica.

The English notes of Folkways SFW CD 40548 say folk harpist José del Rosario Diarte composed this Paraguayan polca. The copyright line printed with the track list credits Félix Pérez Cardozo. The notes are followed for the composer, and the conflicting credit is recorded here. No composition year is given. Carretaguy is explained in the booklet as a Guaraní title for life under the cart.

Recorded by Los Kjarkas in 1981 for Canto a la mujer de mi pueblo and issued as the B-side of a 1982 single. English Wikipedia calls the genre Afro-Bolivian saya and credits Ulises Hermosa and Gonzalo Hermosa. Spanish Wikipedia's infobox has also called it caporales. El País reports the later unauthorised use by Kaoma as Lambada (1989). Year is the 1981 recording.

songwriter: Jorge Carrera Andrade, Jorge Enrique Adoum, Hugo Alemán, Jaime Valencia
research_notes: Danzante written on the night of 7 November 1950 at the house of Oswaldo Guayasamín. Music by Gonzalo Benítez; the lyric is by the poets named in the songwriter field. Spanish Wikipedia, the Universidad Andina Simón Bolívar journal and the Dúo Benítez-Valencia article agree. The duo's recording is dated 1956. Year is the 1950 writing night.

Pasacalle. El Comercio and the Museo del Pasillo say Alfredo Carpio Flores registered the music on 18 January 1947. The lyric is attributed to Luis Alberto Valencia, who recorded it in 1947. Also called Chullita quiteño. The lyric credit is journalistic rather than a registry line, so the record stays Partially verified.

Pasillo by the Quito composer César Guerrero Tamayo. Spanish Wikipedia, the Museo del Pasillo and a 2004 El Universo letter agree on the author. The date is disputed: one account says 1930, and Julio Pazos Barrera has said it was already circulating in 1918. It may have been written while Guerrero lived in Pasto, Colombia. Year is empty. The song is filed under Ecuador, his country.

The anthology Pasillos y pasilleros del Ecuador lists El alma en los labios with lyric by Medardo Ángel Silva and music by Francisco Paredes Herrera. No year is printed in the contents entry consulted. A second page used in this batch documents Ecuadorian pasillo as a genre and does not discuss this title.

The same anthology lists the pasillo El beso as lyric and music by Ramón Moya Alzamora (Quito, 1897–1963) and says he directed La Lira Quiteña, organised in 1925. No composition year for El beso is stated in the passage consulted.
The anthology's contents list Cumandá with lyric by Benjamín Ruiz y Gómez and music by Estanislao Pesantez. No year is given in that entry. Only this contents credit was used.

Dave Martins has written that he composed the song in Guyana in the 1970s at the Pegasus hotel after Pat Cameron of Radio Demerara asked him for a song about the country. Tourism Guyana calls the Tradewinds a Caribbean string band and says the song became an anthem during the Essequibo dispute. BBC Radio 3 lists it as a Guyanese heritage track. No exact year is stated. The song does not name Venezuela.

Dutch Wikipedia says Julius Theodoor Hugo Uiterloo, known as Lieve Hugo, from Paramaribo, performed Langa Bere at the Holland Festival in the Concertgebouw in Amsterdam in 1970. English Wikipedia identifies him as a kaseko singer. The composer of this title is not stated. Year is the documented performance year. Lyric language is not stated on the pages consulted.

Dutch Wikipedia calls Srefidensi his song and says it placed ninth in a 2013 public Srefidensi Top 38 marking 38 years of Surinamese independence. No composition or recording year is given. The 2013 date is the poll, not the song.

Spanish Wikipedia lists Chacarera del rancho among songs Los Hermanos Ábalos, formed in Santiago del Estero in 1939, brought into the Argentine folk repertoire. A performers' note says Adolfo Ábalos registered it at SADAIC in 1968; the same document's layout also shows a 1965 SADAIC line that is hard to assign. A folklore blog places the music in the late 1950s in Mar del Plata and the lyric later. Year is empty because those dates conflict. The group used voices, guitars, piano and bombo legüero.

LetrasTango and Bibletango date the milonga to 1931, music by Sebastián Piana and lyric by Homero Manzi, and say Mercedes Simone premiered it and recorded it for Victor in October 1932. MusicBrainz dates the composer and lyricist credits to 1932. Year 1931 follows the composition date used by LetrasTango. The record is Partially verified because of the 1932 database date.

Composed by Roberto Ternán of Salta in the early 1970s after he met a Uruguayan dancer, José, in the Buceo neighbourhood of Montevideo. Los Tucu Tucu recorded it in 1973. Illapu's Andean arrangement, with quena and charango, is on Despedida del pueblo (1976) and is the version La Tercera and a choral-score note describe as the widely known one. Year is that 1976 recording. The composer is Argentine; the rhythm is Uruguayan candombe. This is not a Rubén Rada song.

Released as a single on 14 August 1992, recorded in July 1992 at WR studio in Salvador, produced by Liminha. Portuguese Wikipedia says Tote Gira (Antônio Jorge Souza dos Santos) wrote it and Daniela Mercury changed part of the lyric; the registered credit names both. A Rede Bahia interview quotes Tote Gira saying he wrote it in 1990 and Mercury recorded it in 1992. Year is the single year. The song is described as the recording that carried axé, then discussed as samba-reggae, across Brazil.

Funk carioca by MC Bob Rum (Moysés Osmar da Silva). The Portuguese song article says 1994. The English article and Bob Rum's biography tie the national success to the Som Livre compilation Rap Brasil Vol. 2 in 1995. Year 1995 is that compilation. The lyric uses the surname Silva for a favela resident. Letras.com also credits the writing to Bob Rum; that lyric page is not used as a source for the text.

title_original: Don't Dilly Dally on the Way
research_notes: Also known as 'My Old Man (Said Follow the Van)' and 'The Cock Linnet Song'. 1919 is the publication/copyright year (B. Feldman & Co., London). Marie Lloyd introduced it on stage c. 1918 but never recorded it; later recorded by Lily Morris and others. Published piano/vocal sheet music is documented (mfiles.co.uk). Genre 'Music hall' is not yet in the taxonomy.

composer: Lonnie Donegan | Peter Buchanan | Beverly Thorn
research_notes: Release year 1960 (Pye 7N 15256, 16 March 1960), recorded live at the Gaumont, Doncaster, 20 February 1960. UK No. 1 for four weeks. Credited writers per Wikipedia: Donegan, Buchanan, Thorn; the song draws on an older music-hall/folk comic tradition. B-side was the English folk song 'The Golden Vanity'. Genre 'Skiffle' not yet in taxonomy.
Single released 5 May 1967 (Pye 7N 17321), UK No. 2; later on the album 'Something Else by the Kinks'. Written and produced by Ray Davies. BBC notes it began as 'Liverpool Sunset'.

composer: Paul Cook | Steve Jones | Glen Matlock | John Lydon
original_instruments: Vocals | Electric guitar | Bass guitar | Drums
research_notes: Debut single, released 26 November 1976 on EMI (EMI 2566), recorded at Wessex Studios October 1976, produced by Chris Thomas. Peaked at UK No. 38 before EMI withdrew it. Writing credit Cook/Jones/Matlock/Rotten (John Lydon) per the official band site.

composer: Ian Curtis | Peter Hook | Stephen Morris | Bernard Sumner
research_notes: Factory Records FAC 23, 7-inch released June 1980 (Discogs: 27 June 1980), a month after Ian Curtis's death; produced by Martin Hannett. Release year 1980.

Written 5 March 1977, released 20 January 1978 (EMI); UK No. 1 for four weeks in March 1978 - first UK No. 1 entirely self-written by a female artist. Year given is the release year. Inspired by Emily Brontë's 1847 novel via a BBC TV adaptation.

composer: Robert Del Naja | Grantley Marshall | Andrew Vowles | Shara Nelson | Jonathan Sharp
original_format: Vocal with electronic production and string orchestra
original_instruments: Vocals | Drum programming | Samples | Turntables | String orchestra
research_notes: Released 11 February 1991 under the temporary name 'Massive' (Gulf War). Vocals by Shara Nelson; strings arranged/conducted by Wil Malone, recorded at Abbey Road. Title is a pun on Schubert's 'Unfinished' Symphony. Trip hop not yet a listed subgenre in the taxonomy.

composer: Jarvis Cocker | Russell Senior | Steve Mackey | Nick Banks | Candida Doyle
research_notes: Single released 22 May 1995 (Island), lead single of 'Different Class'; UK No. 2. Cocker devised the tune on a Casiotone keyboard. Credited to all five band members.

Released 21 November 1994 on FFRR as 'Goldie Presents Metalheadz', vocals by Diane Charlemagne; part of the 21-minute opener of the album 'Timeless' (1995). Audio link is the official Metalheadz label Bandcamp page for the 2017 rebuild (not the 1994 original).

composer: Mark Hill | Craig David | Tony Briscoe
research_notes: Released 29 November 1999 (Public Demand / Relentless, first Relentless release); UK No. 2. Artful Dodger were a Southampton duo (Mark Hill, Pete Devereux).
Debut single, released 26 May 2003 by XL Recordings; UK No. 29. Written by Dylan Mills, female vocal by Jeanine Jacques (musicbase credits). Audio link is the label's own shop page with previews.

title_original: Who Knows Where the Time Goes?
original_instruments: Vocals | Acoustic guitar | Electric guitar | Bass | Drums
research_notes: Written by Sandy Denny c. 1967-68; first recorded on a Strawbs demo sampler. Year 1969 = release of the classic Fairport Convention version on 'Unhalfbricking' (Island ILPS 9102, July 1969). Judy Collins had a 1968 cover.

secondary_associations: Scotland | Isle of Lewis | Ireland (Ulster/Rathlin variant)
research_notes: Late-18th-century Scottish Gaelic love song. Legend (local Uig history society) attributes it to Sìne NicFhionnlaigh / Jane Finlayson (1775-1840) of Tong, Lewis; Wikipedia notes contemporary and 19th-century sources call the author unknown, so attribution is disputed and treated as anonymous here. Earliest identified print: James Logan, The Scottish Gael (1831). An Irish Gaelic variant exists from Rathlin/Ulster.

Composition year 1977 (written on a beach in Brittany while busking); first recorded on the 1979 Alan Roberts / Dougie MacLean album 'Caledonia' (Wikipedia gives single 1978). Often called Scotland's unofficial anthem. Not traditional despite its folk status.

original_instruments: Vocals | Acoustic guitar | Accordion | Fiddle | Mandolin | Pedal steel guitar | Keyboards | Bass | Drums
research_notes: Title track of the 1988 album (Chrysalis), single released 31 October 1988; produced by Pete Wingfield. Instrumentation from MusicFactsDB credits.

Opening track of 'The Cutter and the Clan' (1987, Chrysalis); lead vocal Donnie Munro. Gaelic lyric about land ownership and the absence of a Scottish parliament. Runrig came from the Isle of Skye/Uist and were the leading Gaelic-language rock band.

original_instruments: Vocals | Triple harp | Fiddle | Flute | Guitar | Accordion
research_notes: Released 1983 on Sain (SAIN 1275M) after the 'Taith Macsen' tour with folk band Ar Log. Song about survival of the Welsh language; revived as a Welsh football anthem in 2022. Ar Log instrumentation listed from the album credits; exact instrumentation of this track not confirmed.

Anonymous Welsh love song built from 'hen benillion' (traditional stanzas). Earliest known print of words with tune: 1911 (novel 'Alys Morgan', tonic sol-fa); published by the Welsh Folk-Song Society in 1937. Recorded by Endaf Emlyn (1974), Ar Log (1978), Bryn Terfel and many others.

original_instruments: Vocals | Electric guitar | Bass guitar | Drums
secondary_associations: Northern Ireland | Derry | Belfast punk scene
research_notes: Written summer 1977 by John O'Neill; recorded 15 June 1978 at Wizard Studios, Belfast; released September 1978 on Terri Hooley's Good Vibrations label (GOT 4), reissued by Sire October 1978.

composer: Traditional (air 'Fáinne Geal an Lae' / 'The Dawning of the Day')
research_notes: Year 1946 = first publication of Kavanagh's poem (as 'Dark-haired Miriam Ran Away', Irish Press). Kavanagh himself set it to the traditional air 'The Dawning of the Day'; it was NOT composed by Luke Kelly. The Dubliners recorded it in 1971 (B-side) and on the live album 'Hometown' (1972). Voted Ireland's favourite folk song in a 2019 RTÉ poll.

secondary_associations: Jacobite song | Rebel song | Easter Rising 1916
research_notes: Tune printed in George Petrie's Complete Collection of Irish Music (1855) as an 'ancient clan march' and 'Welcome home Prince Charley'. Jacobite verses (Séarlas Óg) date it to the 1745-46 rising, though that dating is inferred. Patrick Pearse wrote new verses featuring Gráinne Mhaol in the early 20th century. Melody is closely related to 'What Shall We Do with the Drunken Sailor'. Recorded by the Clancy Brothers, the Dubliners, Sinéad O'Connor (2003).

composer: Tommy Potts (first part); older traditional material
research_notes: Three-part slip jig in E minor/Dorian (AABBCC). Credited to Dublin fiddler Tommy Potts (1912-1988), but sources agree the second and third parts are variants of older tunes ('Skin the Peeler', 'Barney's Goat'); Potts probably added/reworked the first part. Potts's recording on 'The Liffey Banks' (Claddagh, 1971); popularised by The Bothy Band's 1975 album. Composition date not documented.

original_format: Vocal with band and string section
original_instruments: Vocals | Acoustic guitar | Electric guitar | Bass guitar | Drums | String quartet
research_notes: Single released February 1993 (Island; Discogs 9 Feb, Wikipedia 15 Feb), from 'Everybody Else Is Doing It, So Why Can't We?'; produced by Stephen Street, strings by the Duke Quartet arranged by John Metcalfe. First song O'Riordan and Hogan wrote together.

original_instruments: Accordion | Bouzouki | Tin whistle | Fiddle | Banjo | Bodhrán | Double bass | Guitar | Mandolin | Drums
research_notes: Not a traditional song: written by American songwriter Steve Earle while living in Galway; recorded in Dublin 1999 with Sharon Shannon and Irish musicians; released 2000 on Earle's 'Transcendental Blues' and Shannon's 'The Diamond Mountain Sessions'. Filed under Ireland because of composition place and strongest cultural association. Mundy's 2008 cover was a five-week Irish No. 1. Not to be confused with Ed Sheeran's 2017 'Galway Girl'.

title_english: Life in Pink / La Vie en rose
research_notes: Lyrics by Piaf, music by Louiguy, registered with SACEM. Piaf recorded it 9 October 1946 for Columbia with Guy Luypaerts's orchestra (fr.wikipedia, Musée SACEM). Single released 1947. First performed live 1946; Marianne Michel recorded it 18 November 1946. Year 1946 is the Piaf studio recording year.

title_english: Lili Marleen (The Girl under the Lantern)
secondary_associations: Soldatensender Belgrad | Marlene Dietrich later version
research_notes: Poem written 1915 by Hans Leip; set to music by Norbert Schultze in 1938; first recorded by Lale Andersen in 1939 as 'Das Mädchen unter der Laterne'. Became widely known after Soldatensender Belgrad began broadcasting it in 1941. Year 1939 is the first recording year.

Released as a single 1 February 1958 (Fonit). Won the Sanremo Festival that night; performed earlier on 31 January 1958 by Modugno and Johnny Dorelli. Italy's Eurovision 1958 entry (3rd). Year 1958 is the release year.

subgenre: Música de intervenção / Portuguese protest song
research_notes: Poem/song by José Afonso. Poem associated with a 1964 visit to Grândola; recorded October 1971 in Hérouville, France, for the album Cantigas do Maio (musical direction José Mário Branco, Orfeu, December 1971). Used by the MFA as the second radio signal of the 25 April 1974 revolution (broadcast 00:20, Emissores Associados de Lisboa). Year 1971 is the recording/release year.

songwriter: Nikolai Nekrasov (poem, 1861) is the literary source of the song text in many accounts; melody folk
research_notes: 19th-century Russian folk song about a peddler and a girl. Wikipedia describes it as a folk song; a piano arrangement is associated with later game use. Year left empty. The Nintendo Game Boy Tetris 'Type A' arrangement (Hirokazu Tanaka, 1989) is a separate video-game record.

songwriter: José Galhardo (Portuguese lyrics); Jimmy Kennedy (later English lyrics 'April in Portugal')
subgenre: Popular song associated with Coimbra (not Coimbra-style fado)
secondary_associations: Capas Negras (1947 film) | Fado de Coimbra (related city, different genre)
research_notes: English Wikipedia fado page and a Redalyc article on Coimbra fado: first recording of 'Coimbra', composed by Raul Ferrão, performed by Alberto Ribeiro in the 1947 film Capas Negras (Amália Rodrigues's film debut). English version 'April in Portugal' (Jimmy Kennedy) 1947. Wikipedia stresses this is a popular song about Coimbra, not Coimbra-style fado. Year 1947 is the film/first-recording year. Filed in europe.csv rather than film_tv because it functions as a Portuguese popular standard; the film is noted.

Composed in 1956 by Charles Dumont, lyrics by Michel Vaucaire. French Wikipedia, English Wikipedia and INA agree that Piaf first recorded it on 10 November 1960; the French article says the Columbia EP came out in December 1960. INA dates her first public performance to 2 December 1960 on Cinq colonnes à la une, the day before her return to the Olympia. She dedicated the recording to the French Foreign Legion. Year 1960 is the recording and release year, not the 1956 composition date.

MusicBrainz lists a recording of Hymne à l'amour dated 2 May 1950, lyricist Édith Piaf, composer Marguerite Monnot, choir Les Chœurs René Saint-Paul, conductor Robert Chauvigny. The French La Vie en rose article mentions the song as a 1949 success dedicated to the boxer Marcel Cerdan, who died that year, which does not match a 1950 composition date and is not used here as the year. Year 1950 follows the MusicBrainz recording date only. A second independent write-up of the song was not opened.

Belgian singer-songwriter Jacques Brel. French, English and German Wikipedia date his recording to 11 September 1959, on the album La Valse à mille temps (Philips). French and German Wikipedia say the music was written with his pianist Gérard Jouannest, who was not credited because he was not yet registered with SACEM. French Wikipedia says the 1959 studio version includes ondes Martenot played by Sylvette Allart, and that part of the melody uses the opening of the second movement of Liszt's Hungarian Rhapsody No. 6. Simone Langlois recorded it in January 1959, before Brel. Brel later called it a hymn to cowardice rather than a love song.

Song by the West Berlin band Nena. German Wikipedia dates the release to 3 January 1983, music by Uwe Fahrenkrog-Petersen, lyrics by Carlo Karges, from the album Nena. The Offizielle Deutsche Charts page dates a CBS 7-inch (A 3060) to 3 January 1983 and names the same writers. English Wikipedia says the German single was released in March 1983 and describes the lyric: balloons mistaken for UFOs start a war. The English-language rewrite 99 Red Balloons (Kevin McAlea) came out in 1984 and is not the record entered here. Year 1983 is the German release.

Title song of Joan Manuel Serrat's 1971 album Mediterráneo (Zafiro/Novola). Spanish and English Wikipedia and Serrat's own site credit him with words and music for this track. The song article says Serrat told El País in 2014 that he wrote it in exile in Mexico, missing the Mediterranean; other accounts place the writing in late 1970. Those origin stories are not used to change the 1971 publication year. Arrangements on the album are credited to Juan Carlos Calderón, Gian Piero Reverberi and Antoni Ros-Marbà. Genre Nova cançó is the name English Wikipedia gives the album alongside cantautor and Spanish folk; the song page itself says canción de autor and names the language as Spanish.

Track 7 of the 1971 album Mediterráneo. English Wikipedia's track list and Serrat's site credit the song to him; the Spanish album article says every piece on the album is his words and music except the lyric of Vencidos. Duration on the English track list is 3:03.

original_format: Vocal with flamenco and rock band
original_instruments: voice | flamenco guitar | electric guitar | electric bass | keyboards | piano | flute | percussion
research_notes: Title track of Camarón de la Isla's tenth studio album, which Spanish Wikipedia dates to 16 June 1979 (PolyGram), produced by Ricardo Pachón. The track uses Lorca's poem from Así que pasen cinco años, adapted by Pachón, who kept the octosyllables. Spanish Wikipedia calls the palo a bambera; English Wikipedia's track list calls it jaleos. Guitars include Tomatito and Raimundo Amador; Rafael Marinelli is credited with piano on the album. El País describes the record as the point where Camarón led a band that mixed flamenco compás with rock arranging. The palo label is disputed between the two Wikipedia track lists, so subgenre is left at nuevo flamenco.

original_instruments: voice | flamenco guitar | electric bass | percussion
research_notes: Track 6 of La leyenda del tiempo (1979). Both Spanish and English Wikipedia credit Volando voy to Kiko Veneno and label it a rumba, duration 3:25. It was also issued as a single in 1979. Camarón sings; the album personnel include Tomatito and Raimundo Amador on flamenco guitar.

Italian Wikipedia: written by Lucio Dalla, published 10 October 1986 on the live album DallAmeriCaruso (RCA Italiana). The album page says the New York Village Gate concert was recorded on 23 March 1986 and that Caruso was a new studio track added for the 10 October release. Dalla said the song came from a stay in Sorrento, in the hotel room where Enrico Caruso had stayed, after the hotel owners told him about the tenor's last days. The refrain quotes the 1930 song Dicitencello vuje. Personnel on Caruso: Dalla (voice, choir), Bruno Mariani (guitar), Roberto Costa (piano, bass, keyboard). Italian Wikipedia files the genre as musica d'autore and canzone napoletana. Piano here is part of the band arrangement, not evidence of a published solo piano edition.

Wikidata describes Barco Negro as a fado based on the Brazilian song Mãe Preta, with new Portuguese lyrics by David Mourão-Ferreira, melody composers Antônio Francisco Amábile (Piratini) and Caco Velho, performer Amália Rodrigues, publication date 1954, language Portuguese. The UCSB discography lists Columbia matrix CL9925, Amália Rodrigues vocal, Portuguese guitar and guitar, lyricist Mourão-Ferreira, composers Caco Velho and Antônio Francisco Amabile, take approximately 1954 in Paris, and marks that date and place as unconfirmed. The Brazilian original is a different lyric; this record is the Portuguese fado. The sources do not say whether it is Lisbon or Coimbra fado.

Italian anti-fascist folk song associated with the partisans. English Wikipedia says the exact origin is unknown; one hypothesis links the melody to a late-19th-century protest song of the mondine, the women who weeded rice fields in the Po valley. It also says there is little evidence the partisan text was sung during the war, and that the text sung today was first published in 1953. Italian Wikipedia says the ANPI treats it as having become an official Resistance hymn only about twenty years after the war, and that it spread after the 1964 Festival of Spoleto. Year is left empty: 1953 is a publication date of a text, not a verified composition year, and the mondine origin is a hypothesis.

composer: Pål Waaktaar | Magne Furuholmen | Morten Harket
songwriter: Pål Waaktaar | Magne Furuholmen | Morten Harket
research_notes: Norwegian band a-ha. English Wikipedia: written by Pål Waaktaar, Magne Furuholmen and Morten Harket. The first version was released on 19 October 1984 (Warner Bros., produced by Tony Mansfield). The hit version, produced by Alan Tarney, was re-recorded for the 1985 album Hunting High and Low and reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100 in the issue dated 19 October 1985. Instrumentation named for the recording includes acoustic guitars, keyboards and drums. Year 1984 is the first release; the internationally known recording is the 1985 remake.

songwriter: Benny Andersson | Björn Ulvaeus | Stig Anderson (lyrics)
research_notes: ABBA single, lead track from the album Arrival. English Wikipedia: written by Benny Andersson, Björn Ulvaeus and Stig Anderson; recorded 4–5 August 1975 at Glen Studio; released in Sweden on 16 August 1976. The official ABBA site gives the same 16 August 1976 Swedish release and says Anderson supplied the title and worked on the lyric with Ulvaeus, with Agnetha Fältskog and Anni-Frid Lyngstad singing. UK Official Charts dates the first chart week to 21 August 1976. The ABBA site mentions Benny Andersson's piano figures in the arrangement. Year 1976 is the single release, not the 1975 session. A later stage version in the musical Mamma Mia! is a reuse, not the origin.

songwriter: Ralf Hütter | Florian Schneider | Emil Schult (lyrics)
original_instruments: voice | synthesizer | electronic drums | organ | piano
research_notes: Title piece of Kraftwerk's album Autobahn. The song article: composed by Ralf Hütter and Florian Schneider, lyrics with Emil Schult, recorded in 1974, album version about 22 minutes, single edit released February 1975. The album articles date the German Philips LP to November 1974. German Wikipedia's album credits list Hütter on voice, organ, piano, synthesizer, guitar and electronic drums, and Schneider on voice, flute, vocoder, electronic drums and synthesizer. Year 1974 is the album; the single is 1975. Piano is listed among Hütter's album instruments, not as a solo piano publication.

Falco (Johann Hölzel, Vienna, 1957–1998). English Wikipedia: single from the album Falco 3, released May 1985 in German-speaking Europe, written by Falco with Rob and Ferdi Bolland, produced by Bolland & Bolland, sung in German. It reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100 on 29 March 1986. The Songlexikon entry says the Bollands wrote the music and a draft text, Falco reworked the words, and the single was issued on 16 June 1985. Inspired by the film Amadeus but not written as part of that score. Wikipedia's May 1985 and the Songlexikon's 16 June 1985 are both 1985 release dates; year is 1985.

original_instruments: voice | electric guitar | bass guitar | drums
research_notes: French Wikipedia: the song appeared in 1977 under Plastic Bertrand's name; music by Lou Deprijck, lyrics by Yvan Lacomblez (Pipou); Deprijck, who produced it, has said he sang it himself. English Wikipedia dates the release to 1978, names the same writers, and says the backing track was Mike Butcher (guitar), John Valcke (bass) and Bob Dartsch (drums). It also reports that a 2006 Brussels appeal court found Plastic Bertrand (Roger Jouret) to be the sole performer, while a 2010 interview in Le Soir, reported by The Guardian, had him say the voice was not his, a statement he then withdrew. Year 1977 follows the French article; the English article's release year is 1978. Vocal credit remains disputed.

Music by Hungarian pianist Rezső Seress, published in 1933. English and Hungarian Wikipedia say his own text was called Vége a világnak, and that the widely known suicide lyric Szomorú vasárnap was written by László Jávor. English Wikipedia says the song was published as sheet music in late 1933 with Jávor's lyric, and that the first Hungarian recording was by Pál Kalmár in 1935. The original musical composition is described as a piano melody in C minor. Piano version exists because the 1933 publication was sheet music, not because a later pedagogical arrangement was found. Urban legends about listeners dying by suicide are reported by both articles and are not treated here as established fact.

Ukrainian Wikipedia: song by Volodymyr Ivasyuk; first public performance on 13 September 1970 in Chernivtsi, on the television programme Камертон доброго настрою, sung by Ivasyuk and Olena Kuznetsova. English Wikipedia says he wrote the song and melody in 1968, inspired by a collection of kolomyikas, and gives the same 13 September 1970 premiere. The Ivasyuk memorial site says he wrote it in 1968 as a 19-year-old medical student. Ukrainian Wikipedia's infobox also says created in 1970 and released 1 January 1971 on Melodiya. Year 1970 is the agreed first public performance; the writing year is given as both 1968 and 1970. Sofia Rotaru's later recording, and the 1971 film of the same name, came after the song.

Russian Wikipedia: song by the Soviet rock group Kino, written by Viktor Tsoi and released in 1991 on the untitled album known as the Black Album. Tsoi wrote it in the settlement of Plienciems near Jūrmala, where he and Yuri Kasparyan were drafting the album; he was killed in August 1990, and the finished album came out afterwards. Reproduktor.net likewise calls it one of his last songs and says the finished version was made after his death. Year 1991 is the album release stated by Russian Wikipedia.

French and English Wikipedia: written and sung by Charles Trenet. He worked out the tune with pianist Léo Chauliac in 1943 on a train between Montpellier and Perpignan, looking at the Étang de Thau; the words draw on a poem he had written earlier. Roland Gerbeau recorded it at the end of 1945. Trenet's own recording, released in 1946, is dated 25 March 1946 by the English article, with Albert Lasry's orchestra, after a rejected take on 19 March. The English-language song Beyond the Sea is a later adaptation, not this record.

English Wikipedia: composed by the Catalan singer-songwriter Lluís Llach in 1968, during the Franco dictatorship, a call to pull together against the stake everyone is tied to. Polish Wikipedia independently dates Llach's L'Estaca to 1968 and says Jacek Kaczmarski later wrote new Polish words to the same melody. The Polish song is a separate record. Instruments are not stated on the pages consulted.

Czech and English Wikipedia: song by Ivan Mládek, recorded by his Banjo Band, first released in 1977 on the album Nashledanou! (Panton). Czech Wikipedia says the text follows an idea from Zdeněk Navrátil, who is sometimes wrongly named as the lyricist; Mládek turned Navrátil's premise into a fairy-tale parody about a man-eater in the swamps near Vizovice. English Wikipedia calls the genre Czech bluegrass; Czech Wikipedia says jazz, Dixieland and comedy. It is filed here as a comedy folk song. A Polish-language craze in 2008 is a later reuse.

Instrumental rumba by Paco de Lucía, opening track of Fuente y caudal (1973). Spanish and English Wikipedia and the Paco de Lucía Foundation agree it was improvised in the studio because producer José Torregrosa said the album was short a piece. Personnel: Paco de Lucía, guitar; Ramón de Algeciras, second guitar; Eduardo Gracia, bass; Pepe Ébano, bongos. The single came out in 1974. Year 1973 is the album. The Foundation notes that the introduction recalls Las Grecas' Te estoy amando locamente and earlier rumbas; those are influences, not a second title for this piece.

Polish and English Wikipedia: Jacek Kaczmarski wrote the words in 1978 to the melody of Lluís Llach's L'Estaca, which he heard in December 1978. It was the finale of the programme Mury, performed with Przemysław Gintrowski and Zbigniew Łapiński. The discography says that programme was recorded in 1980 and first officially released in 1981 on Wifon. In the 1980s it became an unofficial anthem of Solidarity; listeners often dropped the pessimistic last verse. Year 1978 is the year the lyric was written. The Catalan original is a separate record.

Dutch Wikipedia: sung by Wim Sonneveld; Dutch text written in 1965 by Friso Wiegersma under the name Hugo Verhage, on the melody of Jean Ferrat's La montagne; arrangement by Bert Paige. The song is about Wiegersma's birthplace Deurne. The Philips single that charted was released on 18 May 1974, shortly after Sonneveld's death, and reached number 27 in the Netherlands. English Wikipedia (Serbian dances) states Užičko kolo, named after Užice, is one of the most widespread kolo melodies, composed in 1962 by accordionist Milija Spasojević. Year 1962 is the composition year given there. Only that page independently states the composer and year; FolkWorld describes kolo and the Guča festival but does not independently confirm this title. Status therefore Partially verified. Later a standard of accordion and brass (Guča) repertoire.

Antonije Pušić (born Kotor, 1963), performing as Rambo Amadeus, represented Montenegro at the 2012 Eurovision Song Contest in Baku with Euro Neuro. The official contest page credits music and lyrics to Rambo Amadeus and places the song 15th in the first semi-final. English and German Wikipedia describe his work as mixing jazz, rock, funk and satire; the consulted pages do not state the language sung in this song. He has said he used the phrase turbo-folk for his own style in the late 1980s, before it named the later commercial genre.

Winning song of the first Festivali i Këngës, held in Tirana on 21–23 and 26 December 1962. The RTSH festival page credits the song Fëmija i parë to composer Abdulla Grimci and lyricist Dionis Budani, sung by Vaçe Zela. English and Albanian Wikipedia name the song and the 26 December 1962 win.

Montenegro's national anthem, adopted on 12 July 2004. English Wikipedia says it was already a popular folk song whose oldest known version dates to the second half of the 19th century, and that a version was first played in public in 1863 at the National Theatre in Belgrade. The official text is associated with Sekula Drljević, a World War II collaborator, and how much of the text is his is disputed. Music is described as arranged by Žarko Mirković from a traditional melody. Year left empty because 1863, the 19th-century folk versions, and 2004 are different events.

Signature song of Nexhmije Pagarusha (born Pagarushë, 1933), sung in Albanian. Atlantiku and Zëri both credit the music to Rexho Mulliqi and the text to Rifat Kukaj. Labëria News uses the spelling Rexhep Mulliqi for the same composer and identifies him as her husband. No consulted source states a composition or recording year. This is a solo composed song, not an iso-polyphonic piece.

English and Albanian Wikipedia list Oj Kosovë, oj nana ime among Shkurte Fejza's best-known songs and give a 1989 album of that title. The pages do not name a composer. Fejza (born Mushtisht, 18 November 1961) is described as a singer of traditional Albanian folk music whose recordings circulated on tape when they were kept off Kosovo radio and television in the 1980s. Year 1989 is the album year given by both pages, not a separately verified composition date.
Named in English Wikipedia among Fejza's repertoire (Mora fjalë) and in German Wikipedia among selected singles (Mora Fjale). Neither page gives a composer or a year for this title.

Greek Wikipedia states that Fragosyriani was written and recorded by Markos Vamvakaris in 1935, with both lyrics and music credited to him, and that Grigoris Bithikotsis's 1960 recording made it widely known. English Wikipedia also names Frankosyriani among the songs he wrote. Vamvakaris (born Ano Syros, 1905) was himself from the island's Catholic community; Frangosyriani was a name for a Catholic woman from Syros. Instruments are not itemised on the song page consulted.

songwriter: Vassilis Tsitsanis (lyrics) | Alekos Gouveris (lyrics, collaboration disputed)
research_notes: Rebetiko song. Greek Wikipedia credits the music to Vassilis Tsitsanis and the lyrics to Tsitsanis with Alekos Gouveris, and says the first gramophone recording was in 1948 by Prodromos Tsaousakis and Sotiria Bellou on His Master's Voice. Tsitsanis said he began it in occupied Thessaloniki, at one point under the title Matomeni Kyriaki, and finished it in 1948. The University of Ioannina Tsitsanis archive dates a studio recording in Athens to 11 August 1948, in 9/8 zeibekiko, with Tsitsanis on three-string bouzouki. English Wikipedia dates composition to 1943 or 1944 and the first recordings to 1948. Lyric authorship was disputed for years; Tsitsanis later said the words were made with Gouveris.

Instrumental taximi recorded in Athens in December 1946 for His Master's Voice (matrix OGA 1194-1), issued on HMV AO 2726. The University of Ioannina archive and the Melos-project catalogue both credit the composition to Vassilis Tsitsanis and list him on three-string bouzouki, Manolis Chiotis on folk guitar, and an unnamed defi player. Tonality D minor, mode minore, duration 3'16", of which the taximi is 2'55".

secondary_associations: Starogradska muzika | Corfu | Serbian army retreat through Albania
research_notes: Serbian song composed in 1916 on Corfu during the Serbian army's retreat. English, Croatian and Polish Wikipedia agree on 1916 and on a 1917 Columbia recording by the Serbian American group Tamburaško pevačko društvo. Authorship was disputed for decades (Milan Buzin, Dimitrije Marić and Mihailo Zastavniković were among those named). English Wikipedia reports that in 2008 historian Ranko Jakovljević identified amateur musician Đorđe Marinković of Korbovo, who secured authorship rights in Paris in 1922. Sung in triple metre. Often grouped with urban old songs, but it is a wartime soldier song rather than an anonymous starogradska piece.

title_english: Hey, farmsteads in the north of Bačka
research_notes: Zvonko Bogdan (born Sombor, 1942), a Bunjevac singer, wrote the song. English Wikipedia says he recorded it in 1971. A PGP RTB EP, catalogue EP 11054, dated 1972, credits Written-By Z. Bogdan and arrangement and orchestra to Janika Balaž's tamburitza orchestra. RTS quotes Bogdan on writing the words on a bus from Belgrade to Sombor and adding the melody afterwards. Year 1972 is the EP release year; Wikipedia's 1971 date is the recording.

The English-language biography of Ceca (Svetlana Ražnatović, born Veličković, Prokuplje, 1973) says the track Kukavica on the 1993 album Šta je to u tvojim venama became one of her signature hits, and that on this album she began working with Marina Tucaković and Aleksandar Radulović. Croatian Wikipedia dates the album to June 1993 (Produkcija Južni vetar) and says Lucky Sound reissued it as Kukavica. Slovenian Wikipedia treats Kukavica as a September 1993 release. The consulted pages do not name the writers of this particular track, so songwriter is left empty. Ceca's page lists her genres as pop-folk and turbo-folk.

Romanian Wikipedia names Aș renunța (2003) among Nicolae Guță's biggest successes and states that every piece he released through the end of 2003, including those on the album Doamne, ce fericit sunt! (volume 18), was composed by him. English Wikipedia lists Aș renunța among his songs and describes his post-1998 work as manele, a club-oriented Balkan style compared there with turbo-folk and chalga. He was born Nicolae Linguraru on 3 December 1967 and plays accordion. The 2003 date is from the Romanian article only.

Romanian Wikipedia's discography lists Maria Tănase's shellac Electrecord EPA 2190 (1956, 78 rpm) as Ciuleandra, accompanied by Nicușor Predescu's orchestra. The Ciuleandra article identifies the name as a Muntenian folk dance with a speeding tempo, and also as a Tănase record. Her biography describes her as a singer of popular, light, lăutărească and romance repertoire (1913–1963). Year 1956 is the shellac release, not the origin of the dance.

Electrecord shellac EPA 2036 (1956) couples Doina din Dolj, with the text credited to Maria Tănase (t. Maria Tănase), and Văleleu, both with Theodor Cosma at the piano. The same pairing is track 5–6 of the 1956 LP EPD 3. A French-language issue (EPC 138, 1958) titles it Doïna. Year 1956 is the recording release. Piano is the accompaniment on this recording; a separate published solo piano edition was not found in the consulted discography.

The discography lists Columbia shellac DR 198 (1937, 78 rpm) as her earliest recordings by matrix number, coupling Cine iubește și lasă with M'am jurat de mii de ori, accompanied by Costică Vraciu's taraf from Gorj. She recorded the song again in 1943 (catalogue 1477) and in 1956 (EPA 2038 and EPC 110). No author is named. Year 1937 is the first listed recording.

Esma Redžepova (Skopje, 1943–2016) called Čhaje Šukarije her signature song of the mid-1960s and said she wrote the melody and lyrics; English Wikipedia notes that Medo Čun also claimed a share of the melody. Cover.info dates a Jugoton EP (EPY-3112, with Narodni ansambl Stevo Teodosievski) to 1961 and says the sleeve's 'gypsy folk song' credit is wrong. RomArchive documents a 1965 Austrian radio recording and says the song made her a star. Because 1961 and the mid-1960s accounts differ, year is left empty. Romani language is stated by Cover.info and by the song's Romani title. The later use in the film Borat is a secondary association, not the song's origin.

English Wikipedia calls Jovano, Jovanke a traditional folk song from the region of Macedonia, sung in North Macedonia, Bulgaria and Greek Macedonia, about two lovers kept apart by their parents, and naming the Vardar. French Wikipedia gives the language as Macedonian and says Aleksandar Sarievski recorded it in 1958 and sang it through his career; that 1958 date is not in the English article consulted, so it is not entered as the year. Widely adapted; one record is filed under the Macedonian traditional song rather than under a later cover. Leb i Sol's instrumental version is a separate later arrangement and is not given its own record.

Bulgarian Wikipedia lists the compilation Целувай ме+ (2003) in Azis's discography. Gigsty dates the release Целувай ме+ to May 2003 and lists Целувай ме as track 1 (3:44). CritiqueBrainz lists the same 2003 release group and track. English Wikipedia identifies Azis (Vasil Troyanov Boyanov, born Sliven, 7 March 1978) as a Romani singer of chalga, called a Bulgarian form of pop-folk. Writers of this track are not named in the consulted pages.

English Wikipedia says Kazantzidis's first studio recording, in July 1952, was Apostolos Kaldaras's Για μπάνιο πάω, which did not do well, and that Giannis Papaioannou's Οι βαλίτσες, recorded soon after, became his first hit. No exact release year for Οι βαλίτσες is stated, so year is empty. Kazantzidis (Nea Ionia, 1931–2001) is described as a leading laïko singer whose family came from Pontus and Alanya. Greek Wikipedia confirms him as a singer of laïko and rebetiko.

English Wikipedia calls Mantoubala a Kazantzidis original, inspired by the Indian actress Madhubala, and says it was the first record in Greece to sell over 100,000 copies, when the country's population was about 7.5 million. No year is given in the consulted text. The same passage says this turn in his style drew on rebetiko and Indian music and became a template for later Greek popular music.

Greek Wikipedia says that in 1937 Manolis Chiotis recorded his first song, Το χρήμα δεν το λογαριάζω, which became a hit at once, and that he was working in the rebetiko pattern of the time. He is described there as a composer and bouzouki player (born 21 March 1921, died Athens 21 March 1970) who later added a fourth string to the bouzouki. Only this article was consulted for the song. The session instrumentation is not itemised, so instruments are left empty.

Romanian Wikipedia: a widely circulated lăutar dance melody, now played as a concert showpiece rather than a dance, usually on violin and nai. It says Angheluș Dinicu collected and reformulated it, and that he and the violinist Sava Pădureanu made it famous at the 1889 Paris Exposition. A quotation from George Costescu (1944) says a sketch of the melody already existed in Barbu Lăutarul's time and that Dinicu completed it. The same article says the tune also circulates among lăutari in Hungary, Poland and the Balkans, and that one opinion traces it to Central Asia; that origin is not treated as settled. Year 1889 is the Paris presentation, not a composition date. George Enescu later quoted it in the Romanian Rhapsody. Gheorghe Zamfir's English Wikipedia mentions Ciocârlia only as a piece on a 2006 Canadian tour, so he is not entered as the reference performer.

The poem is by Jovan Jovanović Zmaj. Infoprevodi says it is one of 73 poems in the collection Đulići. Serbian Wikipedia lists Тихо ноћи among Serbian starogradske pesme but does not name a composer. Telegraf quotes Mile Bogdanović saying he first sang it on Radio Belgrade on 26 June 1934, as a schoolboy, and again on 19 December 1944 with the Radio Belgrade tamburitza orchestra. The melody's composer is not named in these sources, so attribution is Unknown and instruments are left empty. Year 1934 is that first radio performance, not a publication date of the poem.

Bulgarian Wikipedia calls it a Bulgarian folk song sung by Vasilka Petkova, from the Shop region of Burel, and says it was sung on the wedding night; sowing pepper is the image in the text. Radio Bulgaria says she learned it from her grandfather and that her first Radio Sofia performances date from 1949, and that Ivan Kavaldzhiev later arranged it for choir and orchestra. Year 1949 is that radio date, not the age of the song. Choral arrangements by Kavaldzhiev, Krasimir Kyurkchiyski and others are later versions of this traditional song.

Greek Wikipedia: a traditional Kalymnian tune sung on sponge boats, especially to divers as they came up, to keep them awake and to check for decompression sickness. It says a studio recording was made in 1966 under Domna Samiou's supervision, with captain Pantelis Ginis and a group of men, issued on Fidelity 7375. Dionysios Savvopoulos included an arrangement on Το περιβόλι του τρελού (1969). A prosecutor said in October 1970 that the song was folk; a later court awarded the rights to Ginis and ordered Savvopoulos to compensate him. English Wikipedia's Darla dirladada article says Dalida's 1970 hit is based on this Kalymnos folk song. Year 1966 is the Fidelity single, not the origin of the tune. Authorship remains disputed between the folk classification and the court finding for Ginis.

original_instruments: vocals | saxophone | piano | trumpet | drums | guitar | bass guitar
research_notes: Title track of the 1976 Coconut Records album Zombie, recorded 1976 at Kalakuta Republic, Lagos, with Africa 70 (Tony Allen on drums). UK issue on Creole 1977. Official Fela Kuti site and Discogs confirm Fela as composer/arranger/producer. Year 1976 is the Nigerian release year.

title_english: Mbube (Lion) / later known as The Lion Sleeps Tonight / Wimoweh
secondary_associations: The Weavers Wimoweh | The Tokens The Lion Sleeps Tonight
research_notes: Written by Solomon Linda and recorded 1939 by Solomon Linda's Original Evening Birds for Gallo in Johannesburg (South African Rock Encyclopedia; RFI). Later adapted without proper credit as 'Wimoweh' (The Weavers, 1951) and 'The Lion Sleeps Tonight' (The Tokens, 1961). Do not attribute the original to US adapters. Year 1939 is the recording year.

Originally sung and recorded in South Africa by Makeba's group The Skylarks in 1956 or 1959. International hit is the 1967 US re-recording produced by Jerry Ragovoy (Reprise), released 25 November 1967, with an added English spoken part; Ragovoy then billed as co-writer. Year 1967 is the international-hit release year; the song existed earlier in South Africa.

songwriter: Manu Dibango; S. M. Eno Belinga wrote lyrics for the original A-side football anthem
original_instruments: saxophone | vocals | piano | electric guitar | bass guitar | drums | percussion
research_notes: Recorded 1971, released 1972 (Fiesta, France) originally as the B-side of 'Hymne de la 8e Coupe d'Afrique des Nations'. Atlantic US single 1972. Personnel listed on Wikipedia include Georges Arvanitas and Patrice Galas (piano). Year 1972 is the release year.

title_english: Inta Omri / Enta Omri (You Are My Life)
research_notes: Wikipedia infobox: released February 1964, Sono Cairo; body text says March 1965. Year 1964 follows the infobox; discrepancy noted. Music Mohamed Abdel Wahab, lyrics Ahmad Shafik Kamel. Only one page consulted.

composer: Kwame Asare (Jacob Sam) (1928 recorded version; earlier 1928 versions exist)
original_format: Vocal with acoustic guitars and percussion
research_notes: Kumasi Trio (Kwame Asare / Jacob Sam, H. E. Biney, Kwah Kantah) recorded 'Amponsah Part 1 & 2' in Fante at Kingsway Hall, London, 8 June 1928, Zonophone E.Z. 1001. Afrodisc cites John Collins calling it the earliest version of the archetypal Ghanaian highlife song 'Yaa Amponsah'; the same page notes earlier 1928 versions (Daniel H. Acquaah, 30 January, E.Z. 74; Edmund Tagoe and Frank Essien, 14 March, E.Z. 179). Year 1928 is the recording year. UEW journal: first Ghanaian highlife recorded 1928 in London by the Kumasi Trio (palm-wine highlife).

Wikipedia and the Umm Kulthum archive both date Al-Atlal to 1966. Wikipedia says the lyrics were adapted from poems by Ibrahim Nagi, including Al-Wadaa, and that Riad al-Sunbati composed the melody. The poem itself was published earlier; 1966 is the song performance year given by both sources.

title_english: Alf Leila wa Leila (A Thousand and One Nights)
research_notes: Wikipedia says the song was first performed in 1969, written by Morsi Jamil Aziz and composed by Baligh Hamdi. Shira.net independently lists Alf Leila wa Leila, composer Baligh Hamdi, singer Oum Kalthoum, 1969, lyrics by Morsi Gamil Aziz.

Shira.net credits Mohamed Abdel Wahab, lyrics by Hussein El-Sayed, and says Abdel Halim Hafez and Berlanti Hassan sang it as a duet in the 1953 film Baeat al-Khubz, with a solo performance in the 1957 film Banat al-Youm. The Wikipedia song list names Ahwak among his songs but does not give the year. Year 1953 follows Shira.net only.

Shira.net lists Qariat al Finjan, composer Mohamed el-Mougy, singer Abdel Halim Hafez, 1976, lyrics by Nizar Qabbani, and calls it the final song of his career. The Wikipedia song list includes Qari'at Al Fingan as his last song while alive, without a year on the page consulted.

title_english: Nibtidi Mneen al-Hikaya (Where Should We Start the Story)
research_notes: Shira.net lists the song under Mohamed Abdel Wahab and Abdel Halim Hafez, 1975, lyrics by Mohamed Hamza. The Wikipedia song list names Nebtedi Minen el Hekaya among songs made with Abdel Wahab but does not date it.

title_english: Nour El Ain (Light of the Eye)
research_notes: Wikipedia album page lists the title track with lyrics by Ahmed Sheta and music by Nasser al-Mezdawi, album released 1996 on Alam El Phan. Shira.net also dates Nour el Ain to 1996, lyrics Ahmed Shattah, music Nassar Al-Mazdawi, arranged by Hamid El Shaeiry. Spelling of the lyricist and composer differs slightly between the two sources.

Tarab.ai Masters of Tarab page says Sayed Darwish composed and sang al-Hilwa Di in 1920 for the play Wa-law, with words by Badie Khairi. No second independent source was opened for this title. Later singers named on that page include Fairuz.

Wikipedia album article says Kelmti Horra was released on 24 January 2012 and that the title track was written by Amine al-Ghozzi. The artist article describes it as a protest song of the Tunisian revolution. Both pages are Wikipedia, so the record stays partially verified. Personnel on the album page include guitar, strings and percussion.

Wikipedia: raï song written and performed by Khaled, released 1992 as the lead single from the album Khaled, produced by Don Was. A Discogs master listing returned in search also gives 1992, style Raï, written by Khaled Hadj Brahim. Wikipedia notes a plagiarism case brought by Cheb Rabah that the French Court of Cassation ended in Khaled's favour in 2016.

Wikipedia: written by Jean-Jacques Goldman, performed by Khaled, released 3 August 1996 from the album Sahra; Arabic lyrics by Khaled; French and bilingual versions. MusicBrainz lists the Aïcha single release group as France, 1996, Barclay, taken from Sahra.

English Wikipedia and French Wikipedia both say Dahmane El Harrachi (Abderrahmane Amrani) wrote and performed Ya Rayah in 1973. French Wikipedia says it was the B-side of a 45 with Elli Fat Mat, and that he sang chaâbi with banjo. Rachid Taha's 1997 single is a later cover, not the reference recording.
Cheb Hasni's Wikipedia biography says that in 1987 he and Chaba Zahouania released Beraka (The Shack). Composer credit was not on the page consulted. Single-source record.

MusicBrainz lists Water No Get Enemy on Expensive Shit by Fela Ransome Kuti and Africa 70, Nigeria 1975, Soundworkshop Records. The Wikipedia discography also lists 1975 Expensive Shit with Water No Get Enemy.

Wikipedia discography lists the 1972 album Shakara with the pieces Lady and Shakara (Oloje). Daily Nation describes Lady as Fela Kuti's complaint about women who want to be called ladies rather than women. The Nation article does not give a year. Lyric language was not established from the pages consulted.

Wikipedia says Joromi was released in 1965 by Victor Uwaifo and His Titibitis and was his first gold disc; the same article later says the Philips gold record was presented in 1996. Discogs' artist biography says he had a hit with Joromi in 1969. Year left empty because the two sources disagree. Genre Highlife is on the Wikipedia artist page. Music in Africa describes his highlife variant as akwassa.
Wikipedia lists Guitar Boy among Uwaifo's gold-disc titles, with Joromi, Arabade, the Ekassa series and Akwete music. No release year was on the page consulted.

title_english: One Man's Meat Is Another Man's Poison
research_notes: The song page says Osondi Owendi is an Igbo highlife song written by Osita Osadebe, released and recorded in 1984 on PolyGram. The artist page repeats that the 1984 single was his best-known hit. Both pages are Wikipedia.

Wikipedia: highlife song by the Cameroonian and Nigerian singer Prince Nico Mbarga and Rocafil Jazz, released December 1976 by Rogers All Stars in Onitsha, sung in Nigerian Pidgin, with soukous-style guitar. Discogs lists a Sweet Mother release by Prince Nico Mbarga and Rocafil Jazz dated 1976. Daily Nation also describes the song without a year.

original_instruments: Voice | Sabar | Tama | Guitar | Saxophone | Keyboards
research_notes: Wikipedia album page for Immigrés (1984, recorded 1983-84) lists Immigrés/Bitim Rew as track 1, composed by Youssou N'Dour, genre Mbalax, with Super Étoile de Dakar. Personnel include sabar, tama, guitars, saxophones and keyboards. The album page does not print a language label for this track. Both sources are Wikipedia.

Daily Nation lists 7 Seconds as Youssou N'Dour with Neneh Cherry and says Cherry suggested co-writing an anti-racism song about the first moments of a child's life. No release year or genre label was in that entry. Country filed as Senegal for N'Dour; Cherry's Sweden association is noted only as a secondary association and was not documented on the page beyond her being the duet partner. Songwriter credit is the Nation's co-writing description, not a formal credit line.
Daily Nation calls Taara a 1997 release by Baaba Maal that praises pre-colonial West African leaders including Omar Saidou Tall. The article does not name a genre or a composer. Single-source record.

original_instruments: Electric guitar | Saxophone | Bass guitar | Drums
research_notes: Wikipedia says Utru horas was among songs recorded in 1982 for cassettes and the LP Ken dow werente, and was included on Panorama du Senegal. Songlines spells it Utrus Horas and describes it as the opening tune of the international issue known as Pirates Choice, from a 1982 cassette. Wikipedia describes the band's repertoire as a mix of son cubano, Wolof music and Mande traditions, and says mbalax later displaced them. Composer not stated.

Wikipedia: written in the 1950s by Armando Zeferino Soares; authorship was contested until a December 2006 court ruling named Soares. Cesária Évora popularised it on Miss Perfumado, recorded May 1992 and released June 1992, label Mélodie. Daily Nation describes the migration theme but does not give the year or the songwriter. Year 1992 is the Évora release, not the composition decade.

Daily Nation calls Petit Pays a Cape Verdean morna by Cesária Évora, a homesick tribute to a small country that has morna and coladeira. No year or composer on that entry. Language follows the morna description and Évora's repertoire language on her Wikipedia page, which says she sang morna in Cape Verdean Creole; the Nation entry itself does not name the language.

Salif Keita's Wikipedia page says the 1978 album Mandjou by Les Ambassadeurs Internationaux, recorded in Abidjan, contained the praise song Mandjou for Guinean president Sékou Touré. Music of Mali repeats that Mandjou was their most popular song and helped make Keita a solo star. Both pages are Wikipedia. The song is filed under Mali, where Keita is from; it was recorded in Ivory Coast and addresses a Guinean subject.

original_instruments: Kora | Bolon | Conga | Djembé | Balafon | Brass
research_notes: French Wikipedia: written and composed by Mory Kanté, Manding text, recorded 1987, single 1988 from the album Akwaba Beach (1987), produced by Nick Patrick for Barclay. Instruments named there include kora, bolon, conga, djembé, balafon, choir and brass. An earlier version was on Mory Kanté à Paris. Daily Nation describes the song as a love song mixing Malinke and other languages but does not give the year. Year 1988 is the single year from French Wikipedia only.

Oumou Sangaré's Wikipedia page says her first album Moussoulou (Women) was recorded for Samassa Records and that she became famous in 1989 with its release; World Circuit later re-released it. Music of Mali says the same and describes modern wassoulou as based on the kamalengoni harp. This record uses the album title because no separate single title was verified. Both sources are Wikipedia.

Ali Farka Touré's Wikipedia page names Ai Du as a song of his used in the films L'Auberge espagnole (2002) and Unfaithful (2002). It does not give a composition or release year. Desert blues is the genre label on that page. Guitar and voice are his documented instruments, not a track-specific lineup.

World Music Central's note on The Rough Guide to African Guitar Legends lists Ali Farka Touré: Penda Yoro. His Wikipedia page identifies him as a Malian singer and guitarist and a pioneer of desert blues, but it does not discuss this title. No year was found.

artist: Ali Farka Touré and Ry Cooder
research_notes: Wikipedia says the radio show The World uses Diaraby, a collaboration between Touré and Ry Cooder from the album Talking Timbuktu, as a theme. No release year for the album was on the passage consulted.

World Music Central lists Tinariwen: Imidiwaren and says the group's music deals with homesickness, exile and political awakening. Tinariwen's Wikipedia page places the collective in southern Algeria and northern Mali and calls the guitar style assouf, often characterised as desert blues. The compilation note does not give a year. Tinariwen's Wikipedia page names Tamasheq as the group's language, but this title was not checked line by line.

The Rough Guide to African Guitar Legends track list, as printed by World Music Central, includes King Sunny Adé: Ja Fun Mi Dub. Songlines' Nigeria guide identifies him as a jùjú bandleader. No year for this dub title was found. The title is kept as printed, including Dub.

Daily Nation says Agolo is in Fon, by Beninese singer Angélique Kidjo, and quotes her describing it as a call to make way for Mother Nature. Spotify lists Agolo on the album Aye (1994). Composer credit is the Nation quotation that she named the song; a formal credit line was not opened. Spotify did not print a genre.
Daily Nation lists Wombo Lombo as a 1996 Angélique Kidjo song for the spirit of a dance. No composer, language or genre label was in the entry. Single-source record.

MusicBrainz tracklist for 1960-2010: Africa, 50 Years of Music credits Afia to Angélique Kidjo, vocals, recorded and mixed at Avatar Studios in New York, recording engineer Russell Elevado. No composition year. Benin is taken from the Daily Nation profile of Kidjo consulted in this batch, not from the MusicBrainz row.

Daily Nation says Premier Gaou (First Fool) is based on lead singer Salif Traoré's own story. MusicBrainz lists 1er Gaou by Magic System on the anthology 1960-2010: Africa, 50 Years of Music. Neither source printed a release year or a genre name. Songwriter credit follows the Nation's account that the story is Traoré's, not a publisher credit.
Daily Nation calls Chilen Koe a 1995 hit by Monique Seka of Côte d'Ivoire, about loving someone who is deaf. No composer or genre. Single-source record.
Daily Nation identifies Mathey as Marie-Thérèse Kobla of Côte d'Ivoire and describes Ameyatchi as a plea asking what wrong she has done. No year or composer. Single-source record.
Daily Nation describes Clepo, by Mathey (Marie-Thérèse Kobla), as a mother asking men to help raise children. No year or composer. Single-source record.

MusicBrainz lists Baara by Amadou & Mariam on 1960-2010: Africa, 50 Years of Music. Music of Mali names the duo among internationally known Malian acts. No year or genre for this title was on either page.

MusicBrainz credits M'Bifo to Rokia Traoré, with guitar and lead vocals by her, ngoni by Mamah Diabaté, bass by Christophe Minck, mixed in Paris in March 2003. Music of Mali names her among Malian singers. Year 2003 is the mix date on MusicBrainz, not necessarily a first-release date. Griot music is used because the credited ngoni belongs to the Mande ensemble tradition described on the Mali page; the track row itself does not print a genre.

Franco Luambo's Wikipedia page says TPOK Jazz released Mario in 1985, written by Luambo, sung with Madilu, and that it was certified gold in Zaire. His page identifies him with Congolese rumba. Daily Nation says the song was inspired by a Portuguese gigolo and urges Mario to marry rather than live off older women. Lyric language was not printed in the passages consulted. Year 1985 is from Wikipedia; the Nation entry does not date the song.

Wikipedia lists Non (1983) among TPOK Jazz hits. Daily Nation says that after Franco was jailed in 1978 over Helene and Jackie, he wrote Non, first as a reproach to a woman who rejected him, then, with new singer Madilu, as a lament about one-sided marriage. Year 1983 is from Wikipedia only.

Wikipedia lists Mamou, alternately Tu Vois, in 1984, among Luambo-Madilu releases. Daily Nation describes a woman complaining that her friend Mamou blames her for marital trouble. Year 1984 is from Wikipedia only.

secondary_associations: Le Grand Kallé | Independence of the Belgian Congo
research_notes: Wikipedia: written by Joseph Kabasele (Le Grand Kallé) on 20 January 1960, first played at the Hotel Plaza in Brussels on 1 February 1960, released that day, languages Lingala, Kikongo and French, genre Congolese rumba, B-side Naweli Boboto. Daily Nation also says it was composed in January 1960 to celebrate independence and quotes the Lingala-French refrain. The modern country name is used for the Belgian Congo of 1960.

secondary_associations: Emotion | Real World Records | La Sape
research_notes: Papa Wemba's Wikipedia page says the 1995 Real World album Emotion, produced by Stephen Hague, includes Show Me the Way and Yolele, and that he sang primarily in Lingala. Daily Nation calls Show Me the Way a 1995 hit about leaving a life of crime. Both sources agree on the year.
Wikipedia lists Yolele on the 1995 album Emotion and says the vocals on that album were primarily in Lingala. No second source for this title was opened. Composer not stated.

Wikipedia says Wemba co-founded Zaïko Langa Langa in December 1969 and impressed with his composition Désespoir Jules. No separate release year for the song was given. Genre follows the page's description of him as a Congolese rumba singer.

French Wikipedia discography lists the 1997 Sonodisc album Loi, all songs written and composed by Koffi Olomidé, opening with Loi. The English Wikipedia biography says Loi was released in December 1997 and that the title piece became a hallmark of the ndombolo dance.
