Spotify and the Sonodisc catalogue page list the same track order. Spotify's 1 January 1997 date looks like a placeholder beside the December date in the biography.

Daily Nation describes Papa Bonheur as Koffi Olomidé greeting his father by telephone from abroad. No year. Ndombolo is the style named for him on his English Wikipedia page, not a label printed in the Nation entry.

Daily Nation says this 1967 Tabu Ley song is adapted from a dirge and gives the title as the day I die. Attribution follows that folklore note. His Wikipedia page identifies him as a Congolese rumba bandleader but does not discuss this title. Lingala is the Nation's gloss of the title, not a full language statement. Single journalistic source for the song itself.

Daily Nation says Sacramento is from Tabu Ley's 1986 duet with Canta Nyboma. His Wikipedia page establishes him as a Congolese rumba singer but does not mention this title. Single source for the song.

Daily Nation describes Muzina as a late Tabu Ley gospel tune with a dance-floor sebene, exhorting listeners to pray. No year. Musical tradition is Sacred/Religious because the article calls it a gospel tune; the sebene keeps the rumba association. His biography does not mention the title.

Daily Nation calls African Typic Collection a 1984 hit by Sam Fan Thomas about African diversity and says the melody borrows from Franco's Boma l'heure. No genre label or composer credit was printed. Single-source record.

Daily Nation says Zamina mina, also discussed as Zangalewa, was released in 1986 by band members who were in the Cameroon army, in pidgin, French, Douala and broken English. Tsaminamina is glossed as come, and waka waka as walk while working. No composer. Single-source record. Later international adaptations were not documented on this page.
Daily Nation says Awa Awa is from Wes Madiko's 1996 debut album Walenga and calls for living in peace. No composer or genre. Single-source record.

Daily Nation says Ya Jean is on Madilu System's 1993 album Sans Commentaire and describes a woman thrown out of the marital bed because of a dream. Genre is the Congolese popular style of that article's Kinshasa entries; the article does not print the word rumba for this title. Single-source record.
Daily Nation says Nzele is from the 1993 album Sans Commentaire and is about a marriage broken by gossip. Same single-source limit as Ya Jean.
Daily Nation glosses Mamu Wenu as mother-in-law and says Tshala Muana's song tells a domineering mother-in-law off. No year or genre. Single-source record.
Daily Nation describes Karibu Yangu as Tshala Muana welcoming a lover and asking him to bring the bride price. No year. Single-source record.

Daily Nation says Verckys angered the Catholic Church in Zaire in 1971 with Nakomitunaka, which questions why good is depicted as white and bad as black. Composer credit follows the article calling it his composition. Single-source record. Rumba is the article's Congolese popular context, not a printed genre label.
Daily Nation says the 1973 song Ndona is by Georges Mateta Kiamuangana, known as Verckys, and that he wept in the chorus because his mother had died. Single-source record.

Daily Nation glosses Eswi yo wapi as where does it hurt you, sung by Mbilia Bel about a husband who boasts of gifts but disappears when she is ill. No year. She is identified with Tabu Ley's Afrisa on his Wikipedia page, which supports the rumba filing; this title is not on that page.

Daily Nation says the original Nakei Nairobi was released in 1984, about a childhood friend Elodie (Duni) living in Nairobi. It also says that in 1987, after a Kenyan ban on foreign music, Tabu Ley recorded a Kiswahili version addressed to President Moi. This record is the 1984 original. The article translates the title but does not state the lyric language. Single-source record.
Daily Nation glosses Boya ye as leave him and says Mbilia Bel refuses advice to abandon a jobless partner because he is the father of her children. No year. Single-source record.

Daily Nation, quoting founder member Didier Masela, says Kalayi Boeing is about the band flying to Brussels and dancing, with the Lingala phrases tala Boeing and tokobina. No year. Soukous is a cataloguing label for this later Kinshasa dance band; the article does not print it. Single-source record.
Daily Nation lists Nina as Pepe Kalle with Nyboma, about a woman determined to keep her husband. No year or genre label. Single-source record.

Daily Nation says Chandra, from 1990, by Josky and TPOK, tells the listener to speak to someone they love before it is too late. Franco's Wikipedia page names Josky Kiambukuta as a band member but does not discuss Chandra. Year is from the Nation article only.
Daily Nation calls Amour Chercher Amour a 1983 hit by Antoine Manana, also called Papa Disco. No genre or composer. Single-source record.

Daily Nation says Dede sur Mesure is a dedication to Dede Kabaselle, a follower of the band. Papa Wemba's Wikipedia page documents Zaïko Langa Langa as a Kinshasa rumba band founded in 1969 but does not mention this title. No year.

Daily Nation says Wahito is based on Kanda Bongo Man's relationship with Kenyan Rose Wambui Wahito and his deportations from Kenya in 1991. The 1991 date is the deportation, not a verified release year, so year is empty. Genre soukous is not printed in the article. Single-source record.

Daily Nation says Tika Kolela urges Monique to stop crying because he loves her. It mentions the 1987 album Cantique as a different song, not as the source of this title. No year for Tika Kolela. Single-source record.

Daily Nation says Muchana is Swahili for the sun, inspired by Kanda's 1991 deportation from Kenya, and names singers Djena Mandako and Abby Surya and guitarist Nene Tchakou. The quoted line is given in Lingala. Release year not stated. Single-source record.
Daily Nation calls Ndaya a 1976 ballad in which Mpongo Love refuses to share her partner in a polygamous marriage. No composer or genre. Single-source record.
Daily Nation says Shauri Yako is Swahili for it's your problem, sung by Nguashi N'Timbo to his wife Zena Fatou. The article spells the name Nguashi N'Timbo. No year. Single-source record.

Daily Nation says Bavon was Franco's younger brother and that Maseke ya Meme, the horn of a sheep, laments family witchcraft. Franco's Wikipedia page mentions brother Bavon Marie Marie, who died in 1970, but does not discuss this title. No release year. Rumba follows Franco's documented style, not a label on the Nation entry.

Daily Nation says Lusa is how Olivier N'Goma, also called Noli, pronounced his wife Louisa's name, and that the song tells her to ignore gossip. Country Gabon is in the article heading. No year. Single-source record.
Daily Nation says Bane means children and that N'Goma advises them to heed their parents. No year. Single-source record.
Daily Nation quotes the English chorus of La Musique by Rrum Tah of Cameroon, about a village dancing. No year or composer. Single-source record.

title_english: A Man of Experience and Wisdom
research_notes: A Harvard thesis states that Yekermo Sew was first released in Addis Ababa in 1969 on a 45 rpm disc and that Mulatu composed it for a play by Tsegaye Gabre-Medhin, using the minor form of the tizita mode. AllMusic lists the song with release year 1974 and also on Ethiopiques Vol. 4 (1998). Year 1969 follows the thesis; 1974 is recorded there as a conflicting AllMusic date. Instrumental: the thesis discusses it as an instrumental composition.

AllMusic's Rare Grooves: Africa #1 lists Yègellé Tezeta with Mulatu Astatke as composer and primary artist. MusicBrainz credits the same piece to him on 1960-2010: Africa, 50 Years of Music, and a Sounds of the Universe Ethiopiques box lists Mulatu Astatké – Yegele Tezeta. No original release year was established. Instrumental status is the usual presentation of this title on those compilations; a vocal version was not documented here.

Sounds of the Universe lists Mulatu Astatke – Yekatit on an Ethio Jazz reissue page alongside Netsanet and Yekermo Sew. No year or composer credit was printed for Yekatit on the passage consulted. Single-source record.

Wikipedia lists Ere Mela Mela as a 1975 LP recorded with the Ibex Band, rereleased by Crammed Discs in 1986 and as Éthiopiques Volume 7 in 2000. MusicBrainz credits a recording of Erè mèla mèla to Mahmoud Ahmed as writer. The title is both a song and the album title in these sources. Year 1975 is the Wikipedia LP date.
The Sounds of the Universe Ethiopiques 7-inch box lists Mahmoud Ahmed – Mar Teb Yilal Kafesh. No year. His Wikipedia page identifies him as an Ethiopian singer. Single listing for this title.
The same Ethiopiques box listing includes Mahmoud Ahmed – Aynoche Terabu. No year. Single listing for this title.

Daily Nation says Aster Aweke sings Nafkot in Amharic, about a lover who is away, and notes her years of self-exile in the United States. No year or composer. Ethiopian popular music is a cataloguing label; the article does not name a genre. Single-source record.

MusicBrainz lists Feqer Feqer New by Alèmayèhu Eshèté on the East Africa disc of 1960-2010: Africa, 50 Years of Music. The Éthiopiques Wikipedia page names Alemayehu Eshete among singers compiled from 1960s-70s Ethiopian singles. No year for this title.
Sounds of the Universe lists Alèmayèhu Eshèté – Afer Yemegnshale on an Ethiopiques-related 7-inch box. No year.
The same box listing includes Alèmayèhu Eshèté – Chiro Adarie Negne. No year. Single listing for this title.

Sounds of the Universe lists Getatchew Mekuria – Antchi Hoye and Shilela on the Ethiopiques box. The Éthiopiques Wikipedia page names him among the series. Saxophone is the instrument he is known for on that series' shellela recordings, but this listing does not print an instrumentation line. Subgenre Shellela is used because the paired title on the same listing is Shilela. No year.

Sounds of the Universe lists Getatchew Mekuria – Shilela. The Sound Atlas Ethio-jazz page names Shellela besaxophone among defining works associated with this scene and names Getatchew Mekurya as a key artist. The two titles may be related but are not treated as the same recording. No year.
Sounds of the Universe lists Tilahun Gésséssé – Sew Manen Yimeslal. The Éthiopiques Wikipedia page includes a volume devoted to Tilahun Gessesse. No year for this title.
The same box listing includes Tilahun Gésséssé – Sima. No year. Single listing for this title.

Sounds of the Universe lists Ali Mohamed Birra – Awash. Éthiopiques Volume 28 is described on Wikipedia as Great Oromo Music, Ali Mohammed Birra. No year for Awash. Oromo is the series description, not a lyric check of this track.
Sounds of the Universe lists Girma Bèyènè – Yebekagnale. Éthiopiques Volume 30 is described on Wikipedia as Girma Bèyènè and Akalé Wubé. No year for this title.

original_instruments: Piano | Bass | Tenor saxophone | Guitar | Drum machine
research_notes: MusicBrainz credits Heywete to Tèsfa-Maryam Kidané, composer Bahta Gèbrè-Heywèt, arranger Tèsfa-Maryam Kidané, producer Amha Ashèté, with piano by Girma Bèyènè, bass Haylu Kèbèdè, tenor saxophone Tèsfa-Maryam Kidané, guitar Tèklè Adhanom and drum machine Girmay Asmarom. No year. Piano is part of the band arrangement, not a published solo piano version. Amha Eshete's name places the session in the Ethiopian recording scene documented elsewhere in this batch.

MusicBrainz lists Kiseru Parts 1 and 2 by D. O. Misiani and Shirati Jazz. Smithsonian Folklife describes benga as Luo guitar music from western Kenya, and MusicRadar says Shirati Jazz, led by Daniel Owino Misiani, brought benga to prominence. Those pages do not name Kiseru, so the title rests on MusicBrainz alone. No year.

The band's website says Teddy Kalanda Harrison wrote Jambo Bwana with his brothers in Them Mushrooms and that it was released in 1980. Apple Music lists an album Jambo Bwana, genre reggae, dated 1980. Daily Nation says the song was released in 1982 and glosses the title as hello sir, welcoming visitors to Kenya. Year 1980 follows the official site and Apple Music; the Nation date is noted as a conflict.

Daily Nation glosses Nyako Konya as girl, help me, by Les Mangelepa, a lament about marrying young. The photo caption places the band in Nairobi. No year. Saxophone is mentioned only because the caption names a member as super sax, not as the song's lineup. Single-source record.

Daily Nation says Sina Makosa means I have not wronged you, by Les Wanyika, asking why someone wants to kill the singer. The Swahili gloss is the article's. No year. Kenya is the article's placement of the band. Single-source record.
Daily Nation calls Maria Salome a 2001 hit by Tanzanian singer Saida Karoli, in Haya, a tragic love story, and says Ugandan fans nicknamed her from the lyrics. Single-source record.
Daily Nation says Basiima Ogenze, released in 2010 by Jose Chameleone, criticises people who praise someone only after death. No language or genre. Single-source record.
Daily Nation says Alone is from Philly Bongoley Lutaaya's 1989 album Alone and Frightened and is about HIV/AIDS, asking people not to shun the afflicted. Single-source record.
Daily Nation says Nantongo, by Afrigo Band, praises a woman the singer has not seen matched in Lusaka, South Africa or Kampala. No year. Single-source record.

Daily Nation calls Tuleke Tweliire (Obulo Bwaffe), popularly Nakato Leka, a 1993 reggae release in Luganda by Tshaka Mayanja, and says the text is folklore about twins sent to chase birds from a millet field. Attribution follows that folklore statement. Single-source record.

Daily Nation says Tarihinda by Cecile Kayirebwa encourages dancing, singing and reciting poems, and pays tribute to inanga players and other Rwandan artists. The inanga is named as the instrument of the artists she praises, not necessarily the lineup of this recording. No year. Single-source record.

Makeba's Wikipedia page says the 1977 song Soweto Blues was written by Hugh Masekela about the Soweto uprising. Daily Nation agrees: released in 1977, written by her ex-husband Hugh Masekela, a lament for the victims of the 1976 Soweto massacre. Genre is jazz because Masekela's page, consulted in this batch, calls him a jazz composer of anti-apartheid songs including Soweto Blues; the Nation entry does not print a genre.

Daily Nation says Malaika was composed by Tanzanian musician Adam Salim in 1945, that Kenyan Fadhili William was the first to record it in 1963, and that Miriam Makeba recorded it in 1974 and popularised the story of a man who cannot pay the bride price. This record follows the article's claim for the first recording. The composition year 1945 and the 1963 recording year both come from that single article. Swahili is the language of the title as commonly presented in the article's East African setting; the article does not print a language label. Authorship of Malaika is not checked against a second source here.

Hugh Masekela's Wikipedia page says Grazing in the Grass was his number-one US pop hit in 1968 and calls it a pop jazz tune. The page identifies him as a South African trumpeter. Composer credit was not in the passage consulted. Trumpet is his instrument, not a printed lineup for this track. Single-source record for the song.

Wikipedia says Masekela wrote the anti-apartheid songs Soweto Blues and Bring Him Back Home. No year or lyric language for Bring Him Back Home was on the page. The Mandela association is not stated in that sentence and is not claimed here. Trumpet is his documented instrument.

secondary_associations: Marabi | Manenberg township | Anti-apartheid | Dollar Brand
research_notes: Wikipedia: Cape jazz composition by Abdullah Ibrahim, first recorded in 1974, released as Dollar Brand on Mannenberg – Is Where It's Happening. Basil Coetzee plays a saxophone solo. The piece incorporates marabi, ticky-draai and langarm. Named after the Manenberg township. Piano is not itemised in the passage consulted even though Ibrahim is a pianist, so piano_version_exists stays Unknown. Single encyclopedia source.

Flat International, describing the disc Kwela Sax / Big Joe Special, says Big Joe Special was recorded in 1958 and was the first time Spokes Mashiyane played saxophone; the A-side is Kwela Sax. World Music Network's South African popular-music guide also says he set a trend in 1958 with Big Joe Special, his first saxophone recording, after pennywhistle success. Both say sax jive was later called mbaqanga.

Flat International says Mashiyane popularised kwela or pennywhistle jive with Ace Blues and Kwela Spokes in 1954. World Music Network says he was the first to gain commercial success with Ace Blues in 1954. Pennywhistle follows those descriptions of the style before his 1958 saxophone records.

Daily Nation says Kazet, glossed as gazette or cassette, is by Simon Mahlathini Nkabinde with Hilda Tloubatla, Nobesuthu Mbadu and Mildred Mangxola of the Mahotella Queens, and that it celebrates music as a way of sharing news. No year or genre label. Single-source record.

The song article says Weekend Special was released in February 1983 by Brenda and the Big Dudes, written by Melvyn Matthews, produced by Blondie Makhene and Matthews, genre R&B pop. Brenda Fassie was the lead singer. The album article's track table instead lists the writer as Mally Watson. Songwriter follows the song article; the conflict is why this stays partially verified. Both pages are Wikipedia.

Daily Nation says Vulindlela is a 1997 Brenda Fassie song telling gossipy neighbours to open the way because her son has a bride. The English gloss open the gate is a common translation and was not printed as a translation in the article; title_english is therefore only a descriptive gloss and may be removed if too loose. The article does not print an English title. No composer. Single-source record.
Daily Nation says Mama is from Brenda Fassie's 1994 album of the same name and is a tribute to her mother Sarah Fassie. Single-source record.

Daily Nation discusses Homeless and attributes the phrase we are homeless to Joseph Shabalala, comparing it to words a Zulu speaker uses when proposing. The group's Wikipedia page says they sing isicathamiya and mbube and became internationally known with Paul Simon on Graceland. That page was not used to assign Simon a writing credit, because the Nation entry does not name him for this song. Songwriter field records only the Nation's attribution of the phrase to Shabalala, which is not a full credit. No year.

Wikipedia says Jerusalema is by South African DJ Master KG featuring vocalist Nomcebo, lyrics in Zulu, a gospel-influenced house song first released on 29 November 2019. A Burna Boy remix is dated 19 June 2020 on the same page. Both sources are Wikipedia. The article does not call it amapiano.

Daily Nation says Todii is sung in Shona, Ndebele and English, is an HIV/AIDS song, and is taken from the album Tuku Music. Oliver Mtukudzi's Wikipedia discography lists Tuku Music in 1999. The year is that album year, not a single-release date printed beside the song title. The English gloss is the Nation's question what shall we do.

Daily Nation glosses Ndakuvara as I got injured and explains the ox image as a warning that people who have been submissive may rebel. Mtukudzi's Wikipedia page identifies him as Zimbabwean but does not discuss this title. Shona is not explicitly named for this song; the article discusses Shona imagery only for Todii. Language left empty in the field if this note is the caution: the article does not name the language of Ndakuvara.

Wikipedia says Mapfumo created chimurenga and released the album Corruption in 1989, recorded at Shed Studios in Harare by Benny Miller, criticising Robert Mugabe's government. This record uses the album title because a separate title-track credit was not printed. Single-source record.

A Mediapart blog post discusses Bonga's Mona Ki Ngi Xica and says Cédric Klapisch used it in Chacun cherche son chat. It also says the 1972 album Angola 72 is based on semba. Music of Angola says Bonga (Barceló de Carvalho) popularised semba internationally. The blog does not give a year for Mona Ki Ngi Xica. Semba is the style those sources attach to Bonga, not a printed genre label on a record sleeve consulted here.

Daily Nation, which calls Lucky Dube a South African reggae star, says Victims describes freedom fighters killed by oppressors and then turning on one another. No year. Reggae follows the article's label for the artist. Single-source record.
Daily Nation says Remember Me, from 1989, addresses men who leave children with their mothers. Reggae follows the article's description of Dube. Single-source record.
Daily Nation calls God Bless the Woman a 1995 Lucky Dube song praising women. Single-source record.
Daily Nation lists I'm in Love (With a DJ) by Yvonne Chaka Chaka, about radio as company. The title is English in the article. No year. Single-source record.
Daily Nation says Mamaland by Yvonne Chaka Chaka calls Africa a motherland and asks for a united front. No year. Single-source record.

Daily Nation says this Stimela, by Yvonne Chaka Chaka, uses the steam-train name for the slowness of freedom and quotes the Zulu line Thina sijahile. This is not Hugh Masekela's song of the same title, which was not the subject of that entry. No year. Single-source record.

Daily Nation says Kunjani (how is it going) is by Ricardo and Friends, from Ricardo Groenewald's album I Love You Daddy. No year on this entry; a later entry in the same article dates that album's release to Fathers Day 1988, which is not repeated here as this song's year. Single-source record.
Daily Nation says Ricardo Groenewald released his first album, I Love You Daddy, on Fathers Day 1988, sung from a child's point of view. The year is the album release as stated. Single-source record.
Daily Nation calls Isencane a wedding song by Platform One in which a woman says the bride is too young. No year or language name. Single-source record.
Daily Nation says Luvi Wami, also called Lezontaba, means my darling, by Platform One. No year. Single-source record.

Daily Nation says Jabulani is Zulu for rejoice and was inspired by a May 1982 Soweto concert where PJ Powers and her band performed. The 1982 date is the concert, not a clearly stated release year, so it is kept only as the article's date for the event that inspired the song. Single-source record.
Daily Nation says There Is an Answer, by PJ Powers, asks South Africans to share the country and put the past behind them. No year. The title in the article is English. Single-source record.
Daily Nation says Pat Shange's Sweet Mama uses a lover seen dancing in a club as an image of apartheid South Africa. No year. Single-source record.
Daily Nation lists Yellow Mealie by Lumumba with Condry Ziqubu, about households that had to use yellow maize flour when white maize ran out. No year or fuller name for Lumumba. Single-source record.
Daily Nation says Sondela is Ringo Madlingozi's ballad, come close, a promise not to hurt the person he loves. The English gloss is the article's. No year. Single-source record.

Wikipedia: Ojuelegba by Wizkid (Ayodeji Balogun), from the album Ayo, released 17 September 2014, languages Yoruba and English, genre Afrobeats, produced by Legendury Beatz. The title is a Lagos neighbourhood. A later remix with Drake and Skepta is a different recording. Single encyclopedia source.

Jaojoby's Wikipedia page says that in 1987 he contributed recordings to Les Grands Maîtres du Salegy and that Samy Mandeha Samy Mitady, which he composed and performed, made salegy nationally popular. The salegy article calls him the King of Salegy and describes electric guitar, accordion, bass and percussion, which is the style rather than a verified lineup for this track. Malagasy is the language context of salegy on those pages. Both sources are Wikipedia. Year 1987 is the compilation approach date on his biography.

title_english: I Have No Wealth, I Have No Debt
research_notes: Daily Nation says Khadja Nin's Sina Mali, Sina Deni is about being content with neither wealth nor debt. The English gloss follows that summary. No year. Single-source record.
Daily Nation says Sambolera, by Burundian singer Khadja Nin, answers powerful men who decide how others should live. No year. Single-source record.
Daily Nation says Wale Wetu, by Khadja Nin, tells people to stop complaining because others live with worse poverty and do not beg. No year. Single-source record.

From the 1981 album Sözüm Meclisten Dışarı (Türküola), with Kurtalan Ekspres. Music by bassist Ahmet Güvenç, lyrics by Manço; a requiem for his grandmother Nimet Manço (nicknamed Gülpembe). Year 1981 is the album release year.

title_english: Nassam Alayna al-Hawa (A Breeze Blew Upon Us)
research_notes: Written and composed by the Rahbani brothers for Fairuz. Arabic Wikipedia dates the release to 1967 and the film Bint al-Haris (بنت الحارس) to 1967 (Sout el-Sharq). Al-Bustan Seeds project page dates the film 1968; year 1967 follows the Arabic Wikipedia / original vinyl cited there. Filed here rather than in film_tv because it functions as a standalone Lebanese popular song; the film is noted in secondary_associations.

artist: Georgian State Merited Ensemble of Folk Song and Dance (Anzor Kavsadze)
research_notes: Kakhetian three-part polyphonic song dramatising preparations for battle. Cited by UNESCO (proclaimed 2001, inscribed 2008) as a prime example of Georgian polyphony. Voyager Golden Record includes a 2:21 performance by the Georgian State Merited Ensemble of Folk Song and Dance under Anzor Kavsadze (Voyager 2 launched 20 August 1977). Year left empty (traditional). Reference artist is the Voyager/UNESCO-cited ensemble, not a composer.

original_format: Vocal with piano or folk accompaniment
research_notes: Love poem written 1895 by Akaki Tsereteli; music composed the same year by his relative Varinka Tsereteli at his request (English Wikipedia). Widely known in the Soviet Union; translated into many languages. Only one page consulted. Year 1895 is the poem and (per that page) music year. Genre filed as romance because of its art-song/estrada life, not as Georgian folk polyphony.

Also known as Kâtibim. English Wikipedia calls it a Turkish folk song, an Istanbul türkü, about a clerk on the way to Üsküdar, and says many songs outside Turkey use the same melody with competing origin claims. German Wikipedia treats an Istanbul origin in the 19th century as possible, not proven, and notes a 1902 recording by Felix von Luschan. Sazname states that the Turkish-text version is an anonymous Istanbul türkü with no known poet or composer, and that the melody is shared across the late Ottoman and Balkan repertoire. English Wikipedia names Safiye Ayla's 1949 recording as a notable one. Year is empty because no consulted source fixes a composition date. Eartha Kitt's 1953 Uska Dara is a later American adaptation and is not given a separate record.

Persian tasnif. Persian Wikipedia: music by Morteza Neydavoud, poem by Mohammad-Taqi Bahar (Malek al-Sho'ara). First performance at a celebration for the newspaper Nahid on 7 Tir 1306 of the Iranian solar calendar; the first commercial recording, that autumn, was Moluk Zarabi with Neydavoud on tar, on Polyphon. The mode is mahur, with a passage into shur. English Wikipedia calls it an early-20th-century tasnif and a protest song. Sazgah likewise names Bahar, Neydavoud, mahur, and the 1306 Zarabi recording with tar and with violin by Musa Neydavoud. The Gregorian year is not printed in these sources, so the year field is empty; the Iranian year 1306 is the date they give. Later performances by Mohammad-Reza Shajarian are covers of this tasnif.

secondary_associations: Six-Day War | Basque lullaby Pello Joxepe
research_notes: Written by Naomi Shemer for the Israeli Song Festival. English Wikipedia: commissioned by Jerusalem mayor Teddy Kollek as a non-competitive piece; first sung by Shuli Natan on 15 May 1967. After the capture of the Old City on 7 June 1967 she added a verse. The National Library of Israel blog quotes Shemer: Gil Aldema of Kol Israel asked her, at Teddy Kollek's request, in the winter of 1967, and she chose 20-year-old soldier-teacher Shuli Natan, who sang it with her guitar. English Wikipedia also says Shemer later acknowledged that the melody draws on the Basque lullaby Pello Joxepe, which she had heard from Paco Ibáñez, and that Ibáñez did not treat this as plagiarism. Guitar is from Shemer's own account on the NLI blog, not from a session sheet.

title_english: I am on a long narrow road
research_notes: Turkish Wikipedia's song page: written in 1966 by the Turkish folk poet Âşık Veysel (Veysel Şatıroğlu), a türkü in the hüseynî makam in 4/4, from the Şarkışla area of Sivas, registered in the TRT Turkish folk archive as repertoire number 2973. His biography page names the bağlama as his instrument and lists this song among his works. English Wikipedia calls it one of his best-known songs. The 1966 date comes from the Turkish song page only. Bağlama is taken from the biography's description of his instrument, not from a session log for this recording.

Title song of Sezen Aksu's album Gülümse. The Turkish song page says the words come from Kemal Burkay's poem Hadi Gülümse, the music is by Arto Tunçboyacıyan, and the arrangement is by Onno Tunç. The English album page's track list agrees: writer Kemal Burkay, composer Arto Tunçboyacıyan, length 5:03. Turkish Wikipedia dates the album to 29 May 1991 (Coşkun Plak) and the song's video to 9 August 1991; English Wikipedia dates the album release to 16 July 1991. Year 1991 is agreed. This record is the song, not the whole album.

Lead track of Tarkan's album Ölürüm Sana, released 15 July 1997 on İstanbul Plak; the video is dated 10 July 1997 on the Turkish song page. That page and MusicBrainz credit the lyric to Sezen Aksu and the music to Aksu, Tarkan and Ozan Çolakoğlu, arranged by Çolakoğlu. English Wikipedia says the music was credited to Tarkan and that he later said, in a 2006 interview, this had been done without Aksu's consent. The three-way music credit follows the Turkish article and MusicBrainz; the dispute is noted rather than resolved. Also known abroad as Kiss Kiss.

Persian Wikipedia: folk-rock song by Kourosh Yaghmaei, lyric by his university classmate Mehdi Akhavan Langarudi. The song page says it was recorded in the Iranian year 1350 and released on his first album. The album page says the album Gol-e yakh was recorded on 30 Mehr 1352 at Studio Pop and released in 1352 by Beethoven (Iran), and lists the track at 5:14 with Yaghmaei as composer and arranger. Because 1350 and 1352 are both given, and neither page prints a Gregorian year, the year field is empty. A later performance associated with the Googoosh academy is a cover, not this record.

original_format: Vocal with traditional and electronic instruments
research_notes: Hebrew poem by the 17th-century rabbi Shalom Shabazi, opening 'even if the gates of the generous are locked, the gates of heaven are not locked'. English Wikipedia: Ofra Haza sang it on television in 1978 with the Shechunat Hatikva Workshop Theatre; the recording on Yemenite Songs (also Fifty Gates of Wisdom) is from 1984, length 5:18, and a dance remix produced by Izhar Ashdot was released in 1988. The album page says Yemenite Songs was released in Israel in November 1984, recorded August–September 1984, produced by Bezalel Aloni and Benny Nagari, mixing traditional percussion with drum machines and synthesizers. Her official site credits lyrics and music to Shabazi and the arrangement to Benni Nagari. Year 1984 is the album recording. The 1988 single is a remix of that recording.

English Wikipedia and the National Library of Israel exhibition agree that the song was made in Jerusalem in 1918, for the Balfour Declaration and Allenby's capture of the city, by adapting a Hasidic nigun and adding Hebrew words, and that Abraham Zevi Idelsohn intended it for a choir. The NLI says he had transcribed the Sadigura Hasidic melody in 1915 and published it in his Thesaurus. Wikipedia also records a competing claim that his student Moshe Nathanson wrote the words; Idelsohn's own English Wikipedia page still credits Nathanson with the lyric. The Hebrew University Jewish Music Research Centre says the first commercial recording, by Idelsohn's choir, was issued in 1922 on the Polyphon/Polydor Hebrew Palestinian folksong series. Year 1918 follows the composition date given by Wikipedia and the NLI. The lyric credit is disputed, so the record is only partially verified. Harry Belafonte's 1959 Carnegie Hall performance is a later cover. The song predates the State of Israel; it is filed under Israel as Israeli folk, with Jerusalem in 1918 noted.

secondary_associations: Beirut | Concierto de Aranjuez | Ziad Rahbani
research_notes: English Wikipedia names Li Beirut among Fairuz's civil-war songs. Antiwar Songs credits the lyric to the Lebanese poet Joseph Harb, the melody to Joaquín Rodrigo's Concierto de Aranjuez, and the adaptation to Ziad Rahbani, and says Fairuz recorded it on the 1987 album Maarifti Feek. Voice of Lebanon News says the singer Osama Hallaq performed it first, with Ziad Rahbani at the piano, broadcast in 1983, before Fairuz's album version. Year 1987 is Fairuz's album; 1983 is the earlier radio performance. Piano is documented for the 1983 Hallaq performance, not as a published solo edition. This is not a film song. Rodrigo's concerto itself is Western art music and is not duplicated here.

One melody sung with different words in Azerbaijan (Sarı gəlin), Armenia (Sari aghjik), eastern Turkey (also Erzurum Çarşı Pazar) and Iran. English Wikipedia says the origin is contested and that all versions use the Bayati mode. Azerbaijani and Turkish Wikipedia say Asaf Zeynallı wrote it down and arranged it for piano in the early 1930s. That is why a piano version is marked Yes: it is his early-1930s piano arrangement, not a later pedagogical edition. No composition year is known. Filed once, under Azerbaijan, because the Azerbaijani article and the English article's Azerbaijani section document the text and Zeynallı's notation; Armenia, Turkey, Iran and Georgia stay in secondary associations. Alim Qasimov's 2012 Eurovision interval performance is a later use.

songwriter: Traditional Sufi invocations and interpolated verses
original_format: Qawwali party (lead singer, chorus, harmonium, tabla)
research_notes: Several distinct qawwalis share this title. Nusrat's version was composed in the early 1970s and became a staple of his live repertoire; live recordings issued by Oriental Star Agencies after his 1985 UK tour, studio recording 1988 (per English Wikipedia). The refrain is a traditional Sufi dhikr, so authorship of the text is not solely Nusrat's. Year left empty because composition is given only as 'early 1970s'. Sabri Brothers recorded a different 'Allah Hoo' on the 1978 album Qawwali: Sufi Music from Pakistan.

songwriter: Gulzar (lyrics, after Bulleh Shah's 'Tere Ishq Nachaya')
secondary_associations: Dil Se.. (1998) | Raga Megh / Madhumad Sarang
research_notes: From the soundtrack of Dil Se.. (1998), directed by Mani Ratnam. Music A. R. Rahman, lyrics Gulzar after the Sufi poem/song 'Tere Ishq Nachaya' by Bulleh Shah. Sung by Sukhwinder Singh and Sapna Awasthi; recorded at Panchathan Record Inn. Year 1998 is the film/soundtrack release year. South Asian film song, so filed here rather than in film_tv_animation.csv.

subgenre: Kriti in raga Hamsadhvani, Adi tala
research_notes: Kriti by Muthuswami Dikshitar (one of the Carnatic Trinity) in Hamsadhvani, Adi tala, in praise of Vatapi Ganapati at Tiruvarur. Carnatica.net essay (2004) is the source consulted; exact composition year not given there, so year is empty. Common opening invocatory piece after the varnam in Carnatic concerts.

Title song of Raj Kapoor's film Awaara, sung by Mukesh. English Wikipedia credits lyrics to Shailendra and music to Shankar–Jaikishan, and the film page dates the picture to 14 December 1951 and lists the song in raga Bhairavi. The Hindi film-song database Hamraaz lists the same singer, lyricist and music directors for the 1951 film. South Asian film songs are kept in this regional file. Year is the film's release year.

Sufi song in honour of Lal Shahbaz Qalandar of Sehwan. English Wikipedia says no recording or document of the poem is known before the 1950s, while shrine legend attributes an original to Amir Khusrow and a later reshaping to Bulleh Shah. Urdu Wikipedia repeats that legend and says the tune now commonly heard is associated with Ustad Ashiq Hussain. No author or year is entered. Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan later recorded it; this row is the traditional song, not one of his albums. Harmonium and tabla are the usual qawwali pair and are not taken from a single session credit.

title_original: যদি তোর ডাক শুনে কেউ না আসে তবে একলা চলো রে
title_english: Jodi tor dak shune keu na ase (Ekla Cholo Re)
research_notes: Rabindra Sangeet written by Rabindranath Tagore in 1905 at Giridih, first published as Eka in the September 1905 Bhandar, later song 3 of the Swadesh section of Gitabitan. Tagoreweb gives raga Baul, tala dadra, Bengali year 1312, and notation by Indira Devi. Onushilon dates the writing to 26 Bhadra 1312 at Giridih, during the anti-partition movement. A cylinder by Tagore for H. Bose Swadeshi Records, made sometime between 1905 and 1908, is lost. The song is sung in Bangladesh as well as India. Year is the publication year.

Fifth of Tyagaraja's Pancharatna kritis. Telugu text, Sri raga, Adi tala. The pallavi salutes the many great souls. One account says he sang it at once in 1838 after hearing Shatkala Govinda Marar at Tiruvaiyaru. The Pancharatna page records a conflicting Walajapet account that disciples already knew the kriti before Marar arrived, and that it was an early work. Year is therefore empty. Concert accompaniments vary and are not listed.

Nepali folk song. English Wikipedia says Buddhi Pariyar composed it after collecting it around Pokhara, and that Sunder Shrestha and Dwarika Lal Joshi first performed it in 1969, with sarangi, madal and bansuri. A Nepali essay on Nepal Namcha says it is unclear whether Pariyar wrote the song or only collected it, that a firm first-recording date is not documented, and that one Radio Nepal account names Sunder Shrestha with Santosh Basnet rather than Joshi. Year 1969 follows the English Wikipedia release line and is flagged by that conflict. Not a Narayan Gopal song.

Playback song by Lata Mangeshkar for the 1964 Hindi film Woh Kaun Thi?, music Madan Mohan, lyrics Raja Mehdi Ali Khan, label Saregama. Picturised on Sadhana and Manoj Kumar. A line on the song page that the tune is in raga Pahari is marked citation needed and is not used. The YouTube upload of the film sequence repeats the same credits. Year is the film year given on the song page; a day was not stated.

National anthem of Bangladesh. Words by Rabindranath Tagore. Both language editions say the manuscript is lost, so the exact writing day is unknown, and that the melody comes from the Baul singer Gagan Harkara's Ami kothay pabo tare. Bengali Wikipedia, citing Prashanta Kumar Pal, says it was first sung on 25 August 1905 at a Kolkata Town Hall reading and printed in Sanjibani on 7 September 1905; it was in the 1905 book Baul. The first ten lines were chosen as the anthem on 13 January 1972 and adopted officially in 1972. Written at Shilaidaha in Nadia, now in Bangladesh. Year 1905 is the publication year, not a dated autograph. Second song in this file for Tagore.

Patriotic pop song by Vital Signs, sung by Junaid Jamshed. BBC Urdu and the Express Tribune place the PTV commission and the 14 August broadcast in 1987; Urdu Wikipedia says August 1987; Apple Music dates a release 14 August 1987. Lyrics by Nisar Nasik, with Shoaib Mansoor producing and reshaping the refrain. The Tribune says Nusrat Hussain wrote the tune that was kept, after a first tune was rejected. English Wikipedia's infobox says August 1985, which these other pages do not support, so 1987 is used and the status stays partial. Not the state anthem.

March song by Kazi Nazrul Islam, known by the opening চল্ চল্ চল্. Nazrul Kosh says he wrote it in the first week of February 1928 at Syed Abul Hosen's house in Dhaka, for the Muslim Sahitya Samaj conference; it first appeared in Shikha (Baishakh 1335 / April–May 1928) as Notuner Gaan and in the book Sandhya (August 1929). English Wikipedia dates words and tune to 1928. Dadra tala. Adopted as Bangladesh's national march on 13 January 1972. The lyric names a madol. The English page URL redirects from Chol Chol Chol to Notuner Gaan. Year is the 1928 writing, not the 1929 book.

title_english: Pyar kiya to darna kya (Why Fear When You Have Loved)
research_notes: Song from the film Mughal-e-Azam, sung by Lata Mangeshkar with a chorus, music Naushad, lyrics Shakeel Badayuni. The song page dates the release to 5 August 1960 and says it is picturised on Madhubala. The soundtrack page sets it in raga Durga and says Naushad reshaped a folk line from eastern Uttar Pradesh, Prem kiya, kya chori kari hai. Hindi Wikipedia lists the same singer, composer and duration of 6:21. Second song in this file for Lata Mangeshkar.

title_english: Euta mancheko mayale kati (How Much One Person's Love Changes a Life)
research_notes: Sung by Narayan Gopal. Annapurna Post reports composer Deepak Jangam's account that the lyric came from the palace, that he hid the writer's name while making tunes, and that the kept recording was एउटा मान्छेको मायाले कति फरक पर्दछ जिन्दगीमा, made at Music Nepal and paid for by the palace. A lyrics page names the writer as Chadani Shah, the pen name of Queen Aishwarya, and the same composer and label. No year is stated on either page. Nepali adhunik was added to the genre list. His English biography names the album Manche Ko Maya but not this title.

Song from the nurthi play Sirisangabo. Sinhala Wikipedia dates that play to 1903 and lists it among John de Silva's works; it does not print this lyric. Divaina quotes the opening දන්නෝ බුදුන්ගේ and says it is from Sirisangabo. A song blog gives the same lyric, credits the words to John de Silva and the tune to Vishwanath Lawjee, and names a later performance by W. D. Amaradeva. The tune credit and the Amaradeva performance rest on that blog, so the status stays partial. Sinhala nurthi was added to the genre list. Kept in the regional file as a Sinhala stage song.

title_english: Jat gelo jat gelo bole (Caste Is Gone, They Say)
research_notes: Baul song quoted on the Bengali biography of Lalon, opening জাত গেল জাত গেল বলে / একি আজব কারখানা, and ending লালন বলে জাত কারে কয়. The page gives his dates as 1774 to 17 October 1890 and places his akhra at Cheuriya in Kushtia, now Bangladesh. It does not date this song, so the year is empty and the decade is only the century of his life. No second page consulted here prints the same lyric.

Released in Japan 15 October 1961 (Toshiba-EMI). First heard 16 August 1961 on NHK programme Yume de Aimashō. English-market title 'Sukiyaki' has no connection to the lyrics (it is a beef dish). US Billboard Hot 100 no. 1 in 1963. Year 1961 is the Japanese release year.

original_format: Vocal, often unaccompanied or with folk ensemble
secondary_associations: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage | North Korea (shared tradition)
research_notes: Korean folk song with about 3,600 variants of some 60 versions, all sharing a refrain similar to 'arirang, arirang, arariyo'. Inscribed twice on the UNESCO ICH list (South Korea 2012, North Korea 2014). Origin commonly associated with Jeongseon, Gangwon; first mention cited by Keith Howard in a 1756 manuscript. National Archives of Korea notes multiple origin theories and no agreed-upon date. Country filed as South Korea (research source of the UNESCO 2012 file); the song is shared across the peninsula. Year left empty.

composer: Traditional (Edo-period urban melody; Meiji-period koto arrangement)
songwriter: Traditional; present lyrics attached in the Meiji period
research_notes: Edo-period urban melody, not an ancient court piece. Melody arranged by Ongaku Torishirabe-gakari included in Collection of Japanese Koto Music, 1888, for beginning koto students at the Tokyo Academy of Music. Present lyrics attached in the Meiji period; a new first verse published by the Ministry of Education in 1941. Year left empty (traditional melody; 1888 is a published koto arrangement, not the origin).
Jiangnan folk song, usually dated to the 18th-century Qianlong reign (Qing); some argue Ming (pre-1644). Chinese Wikipedia: originally called 鲜花调. Year left empty. Many regional variants.

composer: 湯尼 / 翁清溪 (Tony / Weng Ching-hsi)
research_notes: Originally recorded by Chen Fen-lan, album Dreamland, Li Ge Records, May 1973; also by Liu Guan-lin, November 1973. Made famous by Teresa Teng on Love Songs of the Island, Vol. 4: Love in Hong Kong (Polydor Hong Kong, 19 December 1977). Japanese Wikipedia confirms lyricist Sun Yi and composer Tony (Weng Qingxi). Year 1977 is Teng's reference recording; composition/first recording is 1973.

title_english: Kawa no nagare no yō ni (Like the Flow of the River)
research_notes: Single released 11 January 1989 by Nippon Columbia; recorded 28 October 1988. Lyrics Yasushi Akimoto, music Akira Mitake, arrangement Kōji Ryūzaki. Hibari Misora's last single released in her lifetime. Artist also romanised Hibari Misora.

original_instruments: Ryūteki | Hichiriki | Shō | Koto | Biwa | Kakko | Shōko | Taiko
research_notes: Best-known gagaku kangen piece, usually in hyōjō; banshiki-chō and ōshiki-chō versions also exist. Japanese Wikipedia cites a 966 court exit performance in Fusō ryakki. Origin is disputed (made in Japan, or transmitted from Tang/Khotan). Dance is obsolete. Later Western-orchestra and piano-and-orchestra works use the melody but are separate compositions. Also written 越殿楽.

title_original: プラスティック・ラヴ
original_instruments: Electric guitar | Electric piano | Bass | Drums
research_notes: Album track on Variety, released 25 April 1984 (Moon/Alfa Moon); produced and arranged by Tatsuro Yamashita. Single release 25 March 1985. Japanese Wikipedia names electric piano (Yasuharu Nakanishi), bass (Hiroki Ito) and drums (Jun Aoyama), with Yamashita on guitar. Year is the album release. Artist also romanised Mariya Takeuchi.

title_english: Tsugaru Kaikyō fuyugeshiki (Tsugaru Strait Winter Scene)
research_notes: Single released 1 January 1977 (Nippon Columbia). Lyrics Yu Aku, music and arrangement Takashi Miki. First issued on the November 1976 album 365日恋もよう. Japanese Wikipedia names tenor saxophonist Masaaki Sano on the introduction. Artist also romanised Sayuri Ishikawa. Year is the single release.

Instrumental by Yukihiro Takahashi on Solid State Survivor (Alfa, 25 September 1979); produced by Haruomi Hosono. Japanese single June 1980. A chiptune of the piece was later used as the theme of the 1982 arcade game Super Locomotive; the composition itself predates that game. Official Alfa music video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Yxep-gS-Btg. Year is the album release.

Track on Happy End album 風街ろまん (URC, 20 November 1971). Lyrics Takashi Matsumoto, music Haruomi Hosono, who also sings. Album credits list acoustic guitar, bass, organ and vocals (Hosono) and drums (Matsumoto); recorded 6 September 1971. Later used in the film Lost in Translation; the song was not written for that film. Year is the album release.

title_english: Haru no umi (The Sea in Spring)
research_notes: Koto and shakuhachi duet by Michio Miyagi, composed at the end of 1929 for the 1930 imperial poetry topic. Premiere that year with shakuhachi player Seifū Yoshida at Hibiya Public Hall. Victor recording with Miyagi and Yoshida released December 1930 (NDL). A violin arrangement of the shakuhachi part by Renée Chemet followed her 1932 visit. Year is the composition year stated by these sources. New Japanese music (新日本音楽), not Western art music.

Six-section instrumental danmono for koto in hirajōshi. Traditionally attributed to Yatsuhashi Kengyō (1614–1685). Kotobank and Japanese Wikipedia note that living Ikuta and Yamada versions may not be his own piece and that some Edo sources credit his student Kitajima Kengyō. No exact year is entered. Later played with shamisen, kokyū and shakuhachi.

Hokkaido herring-fishery work song, the okiage ondo of the Japan Sea coast (Shakotan to Yoichi). Unaccompanied in its work form. Around 1935 the min'yō singer Imai Kōzan fitted shamisen and selected verses for stage use. Kotobank traces the call to Aomori stevedore song brought north with the fishery. No composition year.

title_original: 真夜中のドア〜Stay With Me
research_notes: Debut single by Miki Matsubara, Canyon Records 7-inch W-17, released 5 November 1979. Lyrics Tokiko Miura, music and arrangement Tetsuji Hayashi. Also on the album Pocket Park. Year is the single release.

original_instruments: Piano | Strings | Bass | Drums | Guitar | Synthesizer
research_notes: Written by Hikaru Utada. Single released 28 April 1999 (Toshiba EMI); title track of the March 1999 album. Arrangement and strings by Kei Kawano. English Wikipedia describes piano, bass, drums, guitars and synthesizers in the arrangement; a published solo piano edition was not found. Used as the theme of the TBS drama Majo no jōken; the song was already an album track. Year is the single release.

Fourth single by Sheena Ringo, Toshiba EMI TOCT-22010, released 27 October 1999. Words and music by Ringo; arrangement Seiji Kameda. Oricon and Universal Music Japan confirm the date and catalogue number. Used as an ending theme on Nippon TV's FUN; it is her own single, not a commissioned score. Year is the single release.

Major-label debut single, Meldac, 1 May 1987. Words and music by vocalist Hiroto Kōmoto. The band's Wikipedia discography lists the same date. An Oricon product page gives 21 February 1988 for a later catalogue number (10MD-5); the 1987 date is the one used here. Year is the single release.

Lullaby of nursemaid girls from Itsuki, Kuma District, Kumamoto. Kotobank and Japanese Wikipedia agree it is a local moriko-uta. The melody widely known after 1945 was transcribed by Yūji Koseki and recorded by commercial singers (Teru Kiku, 1953) and differs from the village version. No composition year.

subgenre: New music (ニューミュージック)
original_instruments: Piano | Bass | Electric guitar | Drums | Keyboards
research_notes: Written by Yumi Arai (later Yumi Matsutoya). B-side of the single Kitto ieru (5 November 1973) and title track of the album released 20 November 1973 (Express). Official discography credits her piano and Caramel Mama: Haruomi Hosono (bass), Shigeru Suzuki (guitar), Tatsuo Hayashi (drums), Masataka Matsutoya (keyboards). Used in 2013 as a theme for the film The Wind Rises; the song dates from 1973. Year is the album release.

original_instruments: Electric guitar | Drums | Bass | Keyboards | Alto saxophone | Trumpet | Trombone | Tenor saxophone | Baritone saxophone
research_notes: Opening track of Tatsuro Yamashita's album For You (AIR/RVC, 21 January 1982). Lyrics Minako Yoshida; music, arrangement and production by Yamashita. Album credits list guitar and percussion (Yamashita), drums (Jun Aoyama), bass (Hiroki Ito), keyboards (Hiroyuki Namba) and a horn section. Not the 1977 album Spacy. Year is the album release.

Written by Miyuki Nakajima; arranged by Ichizō Seo. First released 7 October 1992 on the album East Asia (Pony Canyon). Session credits on the fan discography list drums (Hideo Yamaki), bass (Yasuo Tomikura) and piano/keyboards (Nobuo Kurata). Single-coupled in 1998 with Inochi no betsumei, then used with a TBS drama. Year is the album release.

title_english: Dorawayo Busanhang-e (Come Back to Busan Harbor)
songwriter: 김성술 (lyrics of 돌아와요 충무항에); 황선우 (Busan adaptation)
research_notes: Associated with Cho Yong-pil. The Busan Encyclopedia of Local Culture says the piece adapts Kim Hae-il's 1971 song 돌아와요 충무항에 (lyrics Kim Seong-sul, music Hwang Seon-u), was included on Cho's 1972 album, and became widely known in a 1976 recording with some lyric changes. Cho's official chronology lists 1975. Year left empty because those dates disagree. The encyclopedia calls the style trot-rock.

Title track of Seo Taiji and Boys' debut album, released 23 March 1992 (Bando; Bugs lists the same date). Words, music and production by Seo Taiji. Album track is the Club Mix. Often treated as the start of modern Korean idol dance music; filed here as hip-hop/dance rather than a later K-pop single. Year is the album release.

Sung by Kim Kwang-seok; words and music by Kang Seung-won. On the fourth album 김광석 네 번째. The Daegu Encyclopedia of Local Culture dates that album to 25 June 1994. Dong-a Ilbo independently identifies Kang as the writer. Year is the album release.

One of the five surviving pansori madang: the story of Chunhyang and Yi Mong-ryong, sung by one sorikkun with a buk player. Encyclopedia of Korean Culture and the National Gugak Center both cite Yu Jin-han's 1754 poem in Manhwajip as the oldest surviving literary witness, and say the piece was already sung by the mid-18th century. Shin Jae-hyo later revised pansori texts. No single composer. A full performance is several hours; famous passages include Ssukdaemeori. Decade marks that documented circulation, not a composition year.

title_english: Erquan Yingyue (The Moon Reflected in the Second Spring)
research_notes: Erhu piece by Hua Yanjun (Abing) of Wuxi. The Abing article says it was composed around the late 1930s and had no fixed title until Yang Yinliu and Cao Anhe recorded it on 2 September 1950, when the name Erquan Yingyue was agreed. The piece page confirms the 1950 naming. Exact composition year is not stated, so year is empty and the decade follows the 'late 1930s' estimate. Abing also left the pipa pieces Da lang tao sha, Longchuan and Zhaojun chusai.

title_english: Yi wu suo you (Nothing to My Name)
research_notes: Words and music by Cui Jian. First public performance 9 May 1986 at the International Year of Peace concert in Beijing Workers' Stadium, with the band ADO; that performance was included on the July 1986 compilation 让世界充满爱. Later on the 1989 album 新长征路上的摇滚 (overseas title Nothing to My Name). Mixes rock with northern Chinese folk elements. Year is the first public performance, not the 1989 album.

On Jay Chou's album 我很忙 (JVR Music, 2 November 2007). Music by Chou, lyrics by Vincent Fang, arrangement by Zhong Xingmin. Won Song of the Year at the 19th Golden Melody Awards (2008); the awards archive and Sina both record that prize. Uses a pentatonic gong-mode melody described on the song page as 宫调式. Year is the album release.

title_english: Hoi fut tin hung (Boundless Oceans, Vast Skies)
research_notes: Cantonese rock song by Beyond. Words, music and lead vocal by Wong Ka-kui; arrangement credited to Beyond and Tatsuhiko Hara (梁邦彥). First on the album 樂與怒, stated as 14 May 1993, recorded April 1993 at Fuji Studio, Tokyo. A Japanese version, 遥かなる夢に, was also recorded. Wong died in Tokyo on 30 June 1993. Only one Wikipedia language edition was opened, so verification stays partial. Year is the album release given on that page.

This record documents the long-song form, not one fixed melody. UNESCO (inscribed 2008; proclaimed 2005, joint China and Mongolia) describes a highly ornamented, free-rhythm lyrical chant with falsetto and a wide range, sung at weddings, a new home, a birth, foal-branding and Naadam, distinct from the short song (bogino duu). A specific named long song was not verified in this pass. Also practised in Inner Mongolia, so China is a secondary association. Country of the record is Mongolia.

Debut single of the Ulaanbaatar band The Hu, formed in 2016. Wikipedia places the song in 2018 and on the 2019 album The Gereg; 7digital lists a Dashka Productions release dated 14 October 2018. The band's own YouTube upload is the audio link. The band describes the style as hunnu rock and uses morin khuur, tovshuur and throat singing; a named songwriter was not on the pages consulted. Individual composer credit left empty.

Min'yō of Esashi, Hiyama, Hokkaido, a designated prefectural intangible folk cultural property. Japanese Wikipedia and the town site trace it to Shinano packhorse song carried north by kitamaebune sailors and fused with Kenryō-bushi; the Agency for Cultural Affairs summary says the same. The standard hon-uta begins かもめの鳴く音に. A seven-line score was fixed in 1911; the Esashi Oiwake Association unified schools in 1935. No single composer. Shakuhachi is the usual accompaniment of the formalized song.

Okinawan children's song in ryūka metre. Author and place of origin unknown, according to Japanese Wikipedia and the Okinawa prefectural site. Tinsagu is the balsam flower; the first verse compares a parent's teaching to dye on the nails. Okinawa designated it the prefectural favourite song Uchinaa kanasaata on 18 March 2012. Texts vary by district. English Wikipedia notes sanshin sheet music. Later used in the film Japanese Story; not written for that film.

Classical shakuhachi honkyoku depicting a crane raising a chick until the parent dies. Kotobank says the composition date is unknown and that many temples transmit different melodies under this name. In Kinko-ryū the related piece is called 巣鶴鈴慕. The shakuhachi article notes that Gorō Yamaguchi's performance of Sokaku reibo is on the Voyager Golden Record. Separate kokyū and jiuta pieces share the title and are not this record. A specialist site's claim that Ihara Saikaku mentions the name by 1687 was not confirmed on the encyclopedia pages, so no year is entered.

title_english: Kimi wa tennen-shoku (You Are Natural Color)
research_notes: Opening song of Eiichi Ohtaki's album A Long Vacation and a 7-inch single, both released 21 March 1981 (Niagara/CBS Sony). Lyrics Takashi Matsumoto, music Ohtaki, arrangement credited to Tarō Bannai. The single cuts the album introduction. Later used in the 2020 film Watashi o kuitomete; the song dates from 1981. Artist name is also written 大瀧詠一. Year is the release date.

original_instruments: Keyboards | Clarinet | Alto saxophone | Tenor saxophone
research_notes: 13th single by Spitz, Polydor, released 10 April 1996 (official site and Oricon). Words and music by Masamune Kusano; arrangement Masanori Sasaji and the band. Wikipedia's personnel list for the recording includes keyboards (Sasaji), clarinet (Jake H. Concepcion) and saxophones. No tie-up at release. Year is the single release. Catalogue numbers differ between the official site (POCH-1985) and one Oricon page (PODH-1305); the date agrees.

Written by Shin Jung-hyeon. Korean Wikipedia dates the track to 25 August 1974 on the band album. The Encyclopedia of Korean Culture says it opened side A of 신중현과 엽전들 1집 (1974), uses electric-guitar and bass riffs, and mixes rock with gugak and folk gestures. Banned 9 July 1975 and lifted 18 August 1987 (English Wikipedia). A film later used the song; it was written as a band track. Year is the 1974 release.

Title song of Yoo Jae-ha's only album, Seoul Records, 20 August 1987. He wrote, composed and arranged the album. English and Korean Wikipedia say this song was first released in 1985 on Cho Yong-pil's seventh album, then sung by Yoo himself because the earlier setting did not match his style. Bugs notes a violin opening. Discogs lists the 1987 LP (SPDR-070) with this as track B4. Year is Yoo's album release, not the 1985 Cho recording.

Title track of IU's EP Real, released 9 December 2010 (Loen). Lyrics Kim Eana, music Lee Min-soo, producer Jo Young-chul. Asia Economy describes violin, brass, guitar and organ solos answering the vocal. Not written as a drama theme. Year is the release date. Artist name IU (Lee Ji-eun).

Martial pipa piece on the Battle of Gaixia (202 BC), told from the Han side. Chinese Wikipedia says a Ming piece called 楚汉 is the early form and that the score titled 十面 was first printed in Hua Qiuping's 1818 pipa collection (10 sections); later scores use the name 十面埋伏 and often 13 sections, of which modern players usually stop at section 10 (Wu River suicide). English Wikipedia agrees on the 1818 printing and the Ming Chu-Han predecessor. No composer. 1818 is a publication date, not entered as a composition year. Paired traditionally with the civil pipa piece 春江花月夜.

Large guqin piece, also called 广陵止息 and associated in qin lore with Nie Zheng's assassination story. Ji Kang (223–263) played a piece of this name before his execution in 263 and said it would be lost. The surviving notation is not securely his: the earliest extant score is in Zhu Quan's Ming handbook 神奇秘谱, which claims a Sui palace source. Tuning is man-shang diao (second string lowered to match the first). Section titles in that score include 取韩, 冲冠 and 投剑. No composition year is entered.

Love song from the Kham region of western Sichuan, built on a local liuliu tune (跑马溜溜的山上) with a Tibetan-derived filler syllable. Chinese Wikipedia says Wu Wenji collected it in 1946 and adapted it under the Kangding title, Jiang Dingxian wrote an accompaniment, and soprano Yu Yixuan sang it publicly in 1947. A competing claim that Li Yiruo of Xuanhan wrote words and music in the 1930s is argued by the Sichuan provincial-chronicles site and rejected, on different evidence, by the Wikipedia article citing the Kangding gazetteer. Authorship is therefore not assigned. No single year is entered. The 1940s decade refers to the circulated concert arrangement, not the folk tune's origin.

title_english: Bāng Chhun-hong (Longing for the Spring Breeze)
research_notes: Hokkien popular song from Japanese-ruled Taiwan. Music Teng Yu-hsien, lyrics Lee Lin-chiu, arrangement Niki Takio, sung by Sun-sun (Liu Qingxiang) for Columbia Records. Chinese Wikipedia says it was recorded in Tokyo in August–September 1933 and issued in early 1934. The National Museum of Taiwan History audio page says recorded September 1933 and issued as a record at the end of 1933 (Columbia 80283). Year 1933 follows the recording; the disc date is given as 1933 or 1934 depending on the source. A 1938 film of the same name came later. Genre name Taiwanese popular song is used because the taxonomy has no Hokkien-pop heading.

Cantonese song by Beyond. Music and Cantonese lyrics by Wong Ka-kui, written in 1990 about Nelson Mandela after his release from prison. Wong's Wikipedia page and the Beyond page both place it on the September 1990 album 命運派對 and record the 1990 Jade Solid Gold best-lyrics prize. A Mandarin version with different lyricists appeared on the April 1991 album of the same name. BBC interviewed Wong Ka-keung on the Mandela dedication. Year is 1990 for the Cantonese release; the exact day 6 September appears on Baidu and is not used.

Track 5 of Eason Chan's Cantonese album U87 (Cinepoly, 7 June 2005). The album Wikipedia table credits lyrics to Wyman Wong (黃偉文), music and arrangement to C.Y. Kong (江志仁), and production to Alvin Leong. Baidu agrees on those credits and the date, and says the working title was Depression. Third plug track of the album. Year is the album release.

This record is the vocal practice, not one fixed melody. UNESCO inscribed Mongolia's khöömei in 2010. A singer holds a drone and a melody of harmonics at once. Two main styles are kharkhiraa (deep, with a subharmonic) and isgeree (whistled overtones). Sung at ceremonies, in the household, while herding, and as a lullaby, learned orally. Origin placed by UNESCO in the Altai of western Mongolia. A separate 2009 inscription covers khoomei as practised in several countries including Inner Mongolia; this record follows the Mongolia nomination.

songwriter: 방시혁 | RM | 슈가 | ADORA | Arlissa Ruppert | Peter Ibsen | Pdogg
research_notes: Lead single from BTS's repackage You Never Walk Alone, released 13 February 2017 (Big Hit). English Wikipedia credits songwriting to Pdogg, RM, Adora, Bang Si-hyuk, Arlissa Ruppert, Peter Ibsen and Suga, produced by Pdogg. The Korean album page lists the same names on track 15. The official music video is directed by YongSeok Choi; the song itself is not a film score, though the video cites literary and film imagery. Year is the single release. Audio URL is the official Big Hit upload returned by search.

Track 10 of Mayday's album 愛情萬歲 (Rock Records, 7 July 2000). The album page says all lyrics and music are by Ashin (Chen Hsin-hung) and arrangements by Mayday. Baidu agrees and says the introduction uses five piano notes. Also used as the ending theme of the TTV serial 俠女闖天關; the song is an album track, not a commissioned score. Named one of the ten singles of 2000 by the Association of Music Workers in Taiwan. Year is the album release.

Guqin piece linked in legend to Bo Ya and Zhong Ziqi, but Chinese Wikipedia says the oldest surviving scores of 高山 and 流水 are in the Ming handbook 神奇秘谱 and are not securely Bo Ya's. By the Tang the old piece had split into two. The version usually played now is the Qing Sichuan qin player Zhang Kongshan's, with the 'seventy-two rolling-and-brushing' passage. Guan Pinghu's recording of the Tianwenge score was placed on the Voyager Golden Record in 1977. This record is 流水, not the separate piece 高山 and not Hou Zuowu's later combination of the two. No composition year.

An upopo (seated song) of the Biratori area, presented by the National Institute for Japanese Language and Linguistics as one of the songs most often sung there. The institute glosses the opening cupka wa kamuy ran as a god descending from the east and alighting on an ash-tree branch. Upopo are sung seated in a circle, often beating a lacquered sintoko lid, sometimes in staggered ukouk. Kotobank and the Ainu-music article describe the form; the named song text is from the institute page only, so the specific lyric attribution is partial. Genre name Ainu music is not in the older taxonomy list.

One of the five surviving pansori madang, distinct from 춘향가. The Encyclopedia of Korean Culture and the National Gugak Center describe Sim Cheong sold as a sacrifice so her blind father might see, then returned as empress. A full telling is about four hours. Famous passages include Beompi jungnyu. Late Joseon writings (Gwanuhui and others) mention the piece; a composition year is not given. Shin Jae-hyo later reworked a text. Sung with a buk.

original_instruments: Alto saxophone | Flute | Piano | Electric piano | Electric guitar | Electric bass | Drums | Percussion | Trumpet | Trombone | Tenor saxophone
research_notes: Title track of Sadao Watanabe's album California Shower, released 25 May 1978; recorded March 1978 in Los Angeles (official discography). Personnel there: Watanabe (alto sax, flute, sopranino), Dave Grusin (piano, electric piano), Lee Ritenour (guitar), Chuck Rainey (electric bass), Harvey Mason (drums), Paulinho Da Costa (percussion), Oscar Brashear (trumpet), George Bohanon (trombone), Ernie Watts (tenor sax). A composer credit was not on the official track list or the Victor reissue page, so attribution is Unknown. Japanese Wikipedia notes the track was also heard in the 1978 TV drama 十字路. Year is the album release. Recorded in the United States by a Japanese bandleader.

Min'yō of Tagawa, Fukuoka, from coal-sorting work songs of the Chikuhō pits. Japanese Wikipedia and the Tagawa library trace the familiar melody to the Ita coal-sorting song, arranged in 1910 by the teacher Ono Yoshika as a shamisen piece and first recorded in 1932 by geisha of Gotōji. The city site prints the seichō lyric that includes 月が出た出た 月が出た / 三井炭坑の上に出た. After 1945 the song spread as a bon-dance tune. 1910 and 1932 are arrangement and recording dates, not a composition year, so year is left empty. Several earlier work songs fed the piece.

original_instruments: Piano | Orchestra | Electric guitar | Bass guitar | Drums
research_notes: Ballad by X (later X Japan). English Wikipedia: single 1 December 1989, CBS/Sony, written by Yoshiki, from the album Blue Blood (21 April 1989). The album page says the track uses a full orchestra arranged by Neko Saito and played by Great Eida Strings, and that Yoshiki wrote words and music. Oricon lists the single as the theme of the Toho film Zipang; the song was already on the April album. Artist credited as X, the name on the 1989 release. Piano is part of the band arrangement; a separate published piano score was not confirmed here.

Opening track of Sanulrim's first album, Seorabol Records, 15 December 1977. Words and music by Kim Chang-wan. The band is the three brothers Kim Chang-wan (guitar, vocal), Kim Chang-hoon (bass) and Kim Chang-ik (drums). The Encyclopedia of Korean Culture names this song as the hit from that debut. Hard rock on the album page. Year is the album release.

Hokkien song sung by Sun-sun for Columbia. Music Teng Yu-hsien, lyrics Zhou Tianwang. The melody began as the 1933 children's song 春天 (words Liao Hanchen); Zhou rewrote the lyric as 雨夜花. Chinese Wikipedia and the Teng Yu-hsien digital archive date the release to 1934. The National Museum of Taiwan History says recorded September 1933 and issued about 1934 (Columbia 80300). Year is the release year. Second record for the singer 純純; the composer already appears on 望春風.

Tajik beyit (folk ballad) of the Pamirs. Chinese Wikipedia says the name is both a red flower and a woman's name, and that the song tells of a poor youth who loves a princess of Kabul and wanders singing. Several oral versions exist. The 1963 film song 花儿为什么这样红 is Lei Zhenbang's slowed adaptation of this tune and is not this record. No collector's date is entered as a composition year.

Solo gayageum form with required janggu, in three to six rhythmic movements, lasting about 30 to 60 minutes. The Encyclopedia of Korean Culture says late-19th-century Kim Changjo (1865–1919) of Yeongam set the framework from sinawi and pansori rhythms, while similar music already existed; eight named schools (ryu) are now transmitted, and the form was designated an Important Intangible Cultural Property in 1968. This record is the tradition, not one school's fixed score. No single year is entered. 1883 is sometimes given as when Kim, then 19, began the form; the encyclopedia treats that as tradition, not a documented premiere.

title_english: Pin pin hei fun nei (I Just Happen to Like You)
research_notes: Title song of Danny Chan's sixth Cantonese album, Warner, August 1983. The song page credits music to Chan, lyrics to Cheng Kwok-kong, arrangement to Joseph Chow, recorded at CBS/Sony Studio in Hong Kong. The album page describes an opening with guzheng and dizi. RTHK Chinese Gold Song of 1983. Not written as a film theme. Year is the album month-year; a day was not given.

This record is the instrument's traditional repertory, not one named tune. UNESCO inscribed Mongolia's morin khuur music in 2008 (proclaimed 2003). A two-string horsehair fiddle with a carved horse head, played solo or with long song, dance, epic and horse ritual. UNESCO notes tatlaga tunes used to tame animals, transmitted orally, and written sources of horse-head fiddles from the Mongol empire of the 13th–14th centuries. A single composition year is not entered.

Shidaiqu written and composed by Li Jinguang, credited on the disc under the pen name Jin Yugu. First sung by Li Xianglan (Yamaguchi Yoshiko) and issued in 1944 by Pathé in Shanghai, according to both the Chinese and Japanese Wikipedia articles. Chinese Wikipedia says Li found the score at a Pathé session after other singers had found the range too wide. A Japanese lyric by Saeki Takao came later. The singer was a Japanese national working in Shanghai; the song is entered under China as a Shanghai popular song. A day of 20 July 1944 appears on Baidu and a video upload, not on the encyclopedia pages, so only the year is used.

Work song of Taketomi Island, Yaeyama, about the beauty Asato Kuyama (1722–1799) and a visiting official. Japanese Wikipedia says yunta were sung without instruments, often as a men's and women's exchange, and that this song is thought to have been joined to a rice-planting song by the early 19th century. English Wikipedia gives the same story. This record is the old song, not the 1934 Columbia version with new standard-Japanese words by Hoshi Katsu and a new melody by Miyara Chōhō, and not the sanshin piece 安里屋節. No composition year is entered.

Words and music by Kim Min-gi. The Encyclopedia of Korean Culture says Yang Hee-eun released it in 1971 on her first album and that Kim included it that autumn on his own first album (Daedo Records). Weekly Hankook describes the Kim recording as piano and strings. Banned in 1975 and lifted in 1987–88. JoongAng dates a first presentation to 28 August 1970; the year entered is the 1971 record. Artist is the singer of the first issued recording.

Guangdong instrumental piece by Lü Wencheng, named as his representative work on his biography page. The piece article says the score appears in Shen Yunsheng's 1938 Qinxian yuepu, in D gong, 2/4. The Hong Kong Windpipe ensemble, working from a Pathé disc, says a 1936 recording (50576b) has Lü on gaohu (then called erhu), Liang Yizhong on yehu, Shao Tiehong on pipa and Lin Haoran on piano, and that a Western-band recording exists from 1935. 1938 is a publication date, so year is left empty. Later used as the first theme of the Hong Kong series Below the Lion Rock; not written for that series. Peng Xiuwen later scored it for a Chinese orchestra.

title_english: Sha si na ge Shijiazhuang ren (Kill That Man from Shijiazhuang)
research_notes: Song by Omnipotent Youth Society. Chinese Wikipedia: lyrics Ji Geng, music and vocal Dong Yaqian, written July 2006, issued on the self-released album 万能青年旅店 on 12 November 2010. The same page describes mandolin in the introduction and trumpet and saxophone at the climax. The YouTube topic upload repeats the 2010-11-12 date and the same credits. Year is the album release, not 2006. Audio URL is the topic upload returned by search, not an independently verified official channel beyond that credit line.

Min'yō of the Tsugaru district, Aomori, one of the Tsugaru mittsu-mono, sung with tsugaru-jamisen and also played as shamisen alone. Japanese Wikipedia says the tune grew from the Hokuriku song Shinbo Kōdaiji kuzushi, and that Kuroishi tells a separate legend tying the name to the 1597 death of the monk Jōen. The Japan Folk Song Association repeats the 1597 story. Old, middle and new performance styles are distinguished. No single composition year is entered, and the 1597 date is a local legend rather than a documented premiere.

Love song sung by Jeon Hye-young of the Pochonbo Electronic Ensemble. Music by Ri Jong-o, using a poem by Cho Ki-chon, who died in the Korean War; Yonhap says the poem dates from just after liberation and that Ri set it in the late 1980s. Release dates disagree: Korean Wikipedia says 1992, English Wikipedia says 1990 with a 1991 vinyl single, and the North Korean arts dictionary dates the work to 1989. Year is therefore empty. A man whistles under a woman's window. Genre name North Korean popular song is not in the older taxonomy list.

Guzheng solo. Chinese Wikipedia gives two accounts: Lou Shuhua (1907–1952) arranged it in the mid-1930s from the old piece Gui qu lai, or Jin Zhuonan (1882–1976) arranged Shandong tunes and taught them to Lou. The circulating Lou score shares its first half with Jin's and has a longer second half of its own. Cao Zheng's transcription of Lou's gongche score spread the piece; a 1941 disc is described on the Guzhengwang summary of a research article. The title quotes Wang Bo's Preface to the Pavilion of the Prince of Teng. Authorship is not assigned to one person, and no year is entered. Later electronic-organ versions used as television cues are separate.

Title track of Jacky Cheung's Mandarin album 吻別, PolyGram, 5 March 1993. The song page and the album tracklist agree: lyrics He Qihong, music and arrangement Yin Wenqi. New song, not a rewrite of an earlier Cantonese hit. Song of the Year at the 1993 Taiwan Golden Melody Awards. The singer is from Hong Kong; the album was a Mandarin release aimed at Taiwan and the mainland. Not a film theme.

Erhu solo by Huang Haihuai. The piece article says he wrote it in 1959 and finished it in 1960, drawing on the Mongolian tune Улаан туг (Red Banner) and its Inner Mongolian form 红旗歌, and that he played it at the 1962 Yangcheng gathering and won a third prize and a new-work prize at the 1963 Shanghai Spring erhu competition. His biography page also dates the piece to 1959. Yangqin accompaniment and plucked-string imitation are described in later accounts of the original. Shen Liqun's shorter 1974 revision, made for Min Huifen, is a different version. Year is 1959.

title_english: Kitaguni no haru (Spring in the North Country)
research_notes: Single by Sen Masao, Tokuma / Minoruphone, 5 April 1977, catalogue KA-1050 in the article body and on his discography (the infobox also prints KA-2035). Lyrics Ide Haku, music Endō Minoru, arrangement Kyō Kensuke. Kotobank agrees on the 1977 release and those credits. A migrant worker remembers a parcel from home. Long-seller prize at the 21st Japan Record Awards. Not a drama theme.

Title song of Chyi Yu's first Mandarin album, Synco, 1979. The album Wikipedia tracklist credits lyrics to Sanmao and music to Li Tai-hsiang, and says the lyric was first called 小毛驢. Apple Music's album note places the record in the Taiwan campus-folk movement and repeats those roles. The month is February on Wikipedia, 9 July on Baidu, and 1 January on Apple Music, so only the year is entered. Briefly banned in Taiwan because the line about a faraway home was read as pointing to the mainland.

The album page lists an orchestral version and a strings version. Issued under the name 王靖雯 in Taiwan. Later used as an insert in the 1995 Hong Kong film 烈火戰車; the song was written for the album. Singapore best-lyric prize in 1994 went to this song.

Eighth single by Matsuda Seiko, CBS Sony, 21 January 1982 (catalogue 07SH 1112 on the Wikipedia page; the official site lists 10EH-3200 for a later issue of the same release date).
