title_english: Chunjiang huayue ye (Spring River Flower Moon Night)
research_notes: Ensemble piece arranged by Liu Yaozhang of the Great Unity Music Society from Wang Yuting's pipa score 浔阳夜月, itself a reworking of the older pipa piece 夕阳箫鼓. The Huain article, written up from Liu's own account, says the arrangement was finished in October 1925 under the provisional title 秋江月 and renamed 春江花月夜 by Zheng Jinwen in spring 1926, with ten section titles. A Sanya University lecture page also dates the Liu and Zheng ensemble version to about 1925. This is not the Tang poem of the same name, and not the solo pipa piece 十面埋伏. Instrument list is the typical sizhu scoring described in the lecture, not a single documented 1925 session sheet. Year is the 1925 completion of the arrangement.

Title track of Anita Mui's fifth Cantonese album, Capital Artists, 7 January 1986, recorded in 1985. Cantonese lyric by Lin Zhenqiang; music credited to Charlie Dore and Julian Littman, an adaptation of Sheena Easton's Strut. Arrangement Luo Di. Jade Solid Gold award for 1985. Other tracks on the album are television or film themes; this title song is the Easton adaptation. Apple Music repeats the 7 January 1986 album date.

Track 9 of Wu Bai and China Blue's album 愛情的盡頭, Magic Stone, 18 June 1996. The album page says every lyric and tune is by Wu Bai and every arrangement is by Wu Bai and China Blue; length 6:31. Baidu's song entry agrees on the date, the credits and Rock Records as the issuing company. The title alludes to Murakami's novel; the song was not written for a film. A different track on the album, Last Dance, was later used in a drama.

title_english: Bengawan Solo (The Great River of Solo)
secondary_associations: Java | Surakarta | Indonesian national song repertoire
research_notes: Written 1940 in Surakarta by Gesang Martohartono (then 23) about the Solo River, in Indonesian rather than Javanese. Kroncong style with Portuguese-influenced urban folk roots. Became widely known during the Japanese occupation and after independence; also popular in Japan and elsewhere in East/Southeast Asia. Year 1940 is the composition year.

Written and performed by Freddie Aguilar. Recorded 1977 at Cinema Audio; released 1978 (Vicor/Sunshine). Finalist in the inaugural 1978 Metropop Song Festival, Manila. Produced by Celso Llarina, arranged by Doming Amarillo. Year 1978 is the release year.

title_english: Rayuan Pulau Kelapa (Solace of the Coconut Island)
research_notes: Patriotic song by Ismail Marzuki. His English biography dates it to 1944. ANTARA News describes a signed score in the Taman Ismail Marzuki collection dated 15 November 1944. A 2025 conference paper says he wrote it in October 1944, during the Japanese occupation, and that Rose Kusumabrata sang it at the 1947 World Youth Festival. The day is not entered because October and 15 November disagree. Not written as a film theme. Later used as a TVRI closedown under Suharto.

The English biography says that career began in 1969 with a Shan-language song on that service, and that he was born Sai Tin U on 23 September 1950 in Langkho. composer: Christina Macpherson (tune, after Thomas Bulch / James Barr)
research_notes: Lyrics written 1895 by Banjo Paterson at Dagworth Station / Winton, Queensland, to a tune played by Christina Macpherson based on her memory of Thomas Bulch's march Craigielee, itself based on James Barr's setting of Tannahill's 'Thou Bonnie Wood o Craigielee'. National Library of Australia confirms the 1895 gathering. Often called Australia's unofficial national anthem. Year 1895 is the composition year. Early performances were with piano or autoharp.

composer: Traditional (communal, Northland / Māori soldiers, c. 1914); published 1919 by Paraire Tomoana and Āpirana Ngata, who did not claim authorship
original_format: Vocal (often with guitar in later versions)
research_notes: Traditional New Zealand love song in te reo Māori, probably communally composed around the start of World War I (1914) in Northland and popularised by Māori soldiers at Narrowneck Camp. Tomoana and Ngata published it in 1919 without claiming composition; they said it 'emanated North of Auckland'. Year 1919 is the publication year, not the origin. Folksong.org.nz notes later parlour piano sheet music.

Third movement of Suite bergamasque (L. 75). Begun around 1890 (originally titled 'Promenade sentimentale'); substantially revised and published 1905 by E. Fromont. LA Phil lists composed 1890. Year 1905 is the publication year of the revised suite; composition began c. 1890. Originally for solo piano.

subgenre: Solo piano / precursor of ambient and minimalism
research_notes: First of three piano Gymnopédies. Whole set completed by 2 April 1888; No. 1 and No. 3 published 1888, No. 2 in 1895. Debussy orchestrated Nos. 1 and 3 in 1897. Year 1888 is the completion and first publication year of No. 1.

The Gymnopédies article says Satie completed the three piano pieces by 2 April 1888. No. 2 is Lent et triste. IMSLP dates the set 1888 (March-April) and says No. 2 was first published in 1895. Gymnopédie No. 1 is already in the file. Year 1888 is the composition year, not the publication year of No. 2. Genre is the title's own form name, Gymnopédie, which the sources use for these piano pieces.

IMSLP lists No. 3 as Lent et grave and dates the set to 1888, with legal deposit of No. 3 in 1888. The Gymnopédies article says the third was published in November 1888. Second additional Satie title; No. 1 was already present.

The suite article identifies Menuet as part of Suite bergamasque and names Clair de lune as the third movement. Clair de lune is already in the file. The Internet Archive scan of the Fromont edition lists Prélude, Menuet, Clair de lune and Passepied, and the BYU catalogue record returned in search gives copyright 1905. Year 1905 is that publication year. The word Impressionism is the taxonomy label for Debussy's piano music of this period; the consulted pages call the work a piano suite and do not use that word.

The Fromont edition on Internet Archive lists Passepied as the last movement of Suite bergamasque. The suite article and the BYU 1905 publication record were also consulted. Clair de lune and, in this batch, Menuet are the other Debussy titles, reaching the three-title cap. Year 1905 is the publication year of the edition, not a separately verified composition year.

secondary_associations: Op. 30 | Royal College of Music | Novello
research_notes: The article says Scenes from The Song of Hiawatha, Op. 30, is a trilogy of cantatas written by Samuel Coleridge-Taylor between 1898 and 1900, and that Hiawatha's Wedding Feast was completed in May 1898 and premiered on 11 November 1898 at the Royal College of Music. Scoring on that page is tenor, choir and orchestra; the solo section is Onaway! Awake, beloved! Words are Longfellow's. The Kenneth Spencer finding aid names the 1898 Novello edition. Country is the United Kingdom because the premiere place named on the page is the Royal College of Music and the publisher named in the finding aid is Novello; the article does not print a nationality sentence. One source cluster, so Partially verified. The 8 November date in the infobox disagrees with the 11 November sentence; the prose date is the one stored.
